This dialectical formulation mitigates risk polarization, enabling a single LLM to yield continuous risk scores grounded in explicit clinical reasoning. Evaluated on three ISMTS benchmarks, TRIAGE achieves an average AUPRC improvement of 3.3% and reduces calibration error by 81% compared to the competitive baselines. An LLM-as-a-judge assessment further shows that our rationales surpass post-hoc explanations from the baseline by 20% in clinical reasoning quality. The source code is available at https://github.com/HyeongWon-Jang/TRIAGE .
rows.pre_filter_rationale: Production-relevant: addresses calibration and interpretability in LLM-based clinical systems, demonstrates concrete engineering pattern (dialectical reasoning for risk grounding) applicable to document intelligence + agentic workflows in healthcare domains.
rows.entry_relevance_reason: While the paper demonstrates LLM application to a structured prediction task with observable improvements in calibration and explainability, the domain is specialized clinical time series prediction rather than core NLP/RAG/agentic work, and the technical contribution centers on prompt engineering for reasoning rather than production system architecture.
rows.entry_value_rationale: The dialectical reasoning pattern for generating competing outcome rationales could inform multi-perspective prompting in agentic systems, and the calibration recovery technique is relevant for LLM-as-judge applications. However, the irregular time series handling and clinical focus limit transferability to document intelligence and retrieval pipelines.
rows.entry_summary: TRIAGE addresses risk polarization in LLM-based clinical risk prediction on irregularly sampled medical time series by using dialectical reasoning over competing outcomes. It generates outcome-specific rationales and derives calibrated continuous risk scores from implicit probabilities, achieving 3.3% AUPRC improvement and 81% calibration error reduction.

rows.title: Decoy-Calibrated Failure Audits for Language Models
rows.abstract: Useful audits reveal not only how often a model fails, but also where its failures concentrate. An auditor may test many candidate explanations: long inputs, indirect questions, distracting evidence, or combinations of these factors. The risk is selection. The largest observed effect may reflect a real failure mode, or it may simply be the best result among many tried. We introduce Janus, a procedure for deciding when a proposed error explanation is credible enough to report. The goal is not to generate new explanations, but to decide which ones hold up. The auditor starts with a fixed model, a labeled evaluation set, and a frozen list of candidate explanations, which we call descriptors. Janus scores each descriptor by its error-rate lift, then compares real descriptors with fake ones that have the same frequencies but are randomly assigned to examples. A descriptor is confirmed only if it beats this decoy floor on the data used for discovery and then repeats on separate held-out data. In a controlled audit of multi-table lookup tasks, Janus identifies the planted failure, confirming long-chain descriptors and their interactions. The LLM often stops partway through the lookup chain instead of reaching the final answer. On two public benchmarks, MuSiQue and LongBench v2, the SliceLine baseline flags plausible high-error pockets, but Janus confirms none of them. Ablations show why both safeguards matter. On LongBench v2, an uncalibrated fixed threshold reports 20 descriptors, the decoy floor leaves one, and the holdout check rejects the last one after its lift shrinks from 0.36 to 0.05. The resulting principle separates proposing explanations from reporting them. Candidates may come from any source, but only those that beat decoys and replicate on fresh data become audit findings.
rows.pre_filter_rationale: Directly applicable to production LLM evaluation workflows; addresses critical problem of distinguishing spurious correlations from genuine failure modes when auditing model behavior—essential for reliable system monitoring and incident diagnosis.
rows.entry_relevance_reason: Directly applicable to production LLM evaluation and observability, addressing rigorous failure mode detection critical for production systems, though tilted toward evaluation methodology over immediate deployment concerns.
rows.entry_value_rationale: Provides a concrete framework for avoiding spurious failure discovery in LLM audits—a key risk when evaluating RAG/agentic systems in production. The decoy-calibration approach prevents overconfident claims about model failures, essential for making reliable deployment and monitoring decisions.
rows.entry_summary: Janus is a procedure for auditing LLM failure modes that separates explanation discovery from reporting. It uses decoy descriptors (fake properties with same prevalence but random assignment) to calibrate error-lift thresholds and requires replication on holdout data before confirming audit findings.

rows.title: INFUSER: Influence-Guided Self-Evolution Improves Reasoning
rows.abstract: Self-evolution offers a scalable path to stronger reasoning: a pretrained language model improves itself with only minimal external supervision. Yet existing methods either depend on extensively curated or teacher-generated training data, or, when the generator runs unsupervised, reward it by a difficulty heuristic that need not improve the solver. We introduce INFUSER, an iterative co-training framework with two co-evolving roles: a Generator that drafts questions and reference golden answers from a pool of unstructured, automatically collected documents, and a Solver that improves by training on them. The solver is trained with standard correctness rewards against the generator-provided answers, while the generator is rewarded by an optimizer-aware influence score that measures whether each proposed question would actually improve the solver on the target distribution. Because this continuous, noisy influence score is poorly served by standard GRPO, we propose DuGRPO, a dual-normalized variant of GRPO, for generator training. Together, these turn the document pool into an adaptive curriculum that favors questions useful to the current solver, not just hard ones. On Qwen3-8B-Base, INFUSER outperforms strong self-evolution baselines with over 20% relative improvement on Olympiad and SuperGPQA benchmarks, and an 8B INFUSER co-evolving generator outperforms a frozen 32B thinking generator on math and coding. Ablations confirm each design choice is necessary, and two extensions, applying INFUSER to an instruction-finetuned anchor and augmenting it with rule-verifiable RLVR data, further demonstrate the flexibility and generalizability of the framework. Code is available at https://github.com/FFishy-git/INFUSER.
rows.pre_filter_rationale: Directly relevant self-improvement framework for LLMs with practical engineering contributions (influence-aware curriculum generation, DuGRPO variant) applicable to production reasoning systems; strong empirical results on math/coding with clear architectural patterns for agentic data generation.
rows.entry_relevance_reason: Self-evolution frameworks and influence-guided training are relevant to agentic system design and LLM improvement, but the paper's focus on synthetic question generation from documents is a narrow application with limited direct production applicability.
rows.entry_value_rationale: The influence-scoring mechanism for evaluating which training examples actually improve model performance on target distributions could inform evaluation strategies for RAG-generated synthetic data or agent feedback loops. However, the co-training pattern is more academic-exploration oriented than directly applicable to production document intelligence or retrieval systems.
rows.entry_summary: INFUSER is an iterative co-training framework for self-evolution where a Generator creates questions from unstructured documents and a Solver improves by training on them. An optimizer-aware influence score rewards the Generator for proposing questions that actually improve the Solver on target distributions, using DuGRPO for stable training.

rows.title: A Unifying Lens on Reward Uncertainty in RLHF
rows.abstract: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) is bottlenecked by reward hacking, where the policy exploits errors in a proxy reward model (RM) and produces high RM scores without genuine quality gains. A natural mitigation is pessimism: lowering rewards in regions where the RM is uncertain. However, standard scalar RMs provide no principled notion of uncertainty. We argue that the right object is a distributional reward model $p(r\mid x,y)$. Under either a Bayesian inference or a KL-distributionally robust optimization (KL-DRO) lens, the KL-regularized RLHF objective admits a closed-form effective reward $\tilde r(x,y) = \pmβ\log\mathbb{E}_p[e^{\pm r/β}]$. The pessimistic branch unifies the prior heuristics for RM ensemble aggregation: mean aggregation, worst-case optimization (WCO), and uncertainty-weighted optimization (UWO) all emerge as limits or truncations of this single expression. This also clarifies the implicit assumptions of each existing rule.
rows.pre_filter_rationale: Directly addresses reward hacking in RLHF—a critical production failure mode—with a unified mathematical framework that explains existing heuristics (ensemble aggregation, WCO, UWO) and provides principled guidance for uncertainty-aware reward modeling in deployed systems.
rows.entry_relevance_reason: Addresses reward model uncertainty in RLHF, which is relevant to agentic system safety and evaluation, but focuses on theoretical unification of existing methods rather than new architectural patterns or production deployment strategies.
rows.entry_value_rationale: Provides useful formalization for understanding reward aggregation heuristics (mean/WCO/UWO) in production RLHF pipelines and reward hacking mitigation, applicable when building reliable agent reward signals. However, limited actionability without concrete implementation guidance for integrating distributional rewards into serving or inference.
rows.entry_summary: Unifying framework for reward uncertainty in RLHF via distributional reward models. Shows that both Bayesian marginalization and KL-DRO yield closed-form effective rewards using moment generating functions, unifying prior ensemble aggregation heuristics (mean, WCO, UWO) as limits/truncations of a single expression to mitigate reward hacking.

rows.title: Late-Layer Fusion is Enough: Dual-Path Vision Token Routing for Multimodal Large Language Models under Visual Saturation
rows.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) commonly inherit the deep, symmetric Transformer backbone designed for unimodal text modeling, and apply the same computation uniformly to image and language tokens. This design overlooks a key modality asymmetry: image and text tokens differ substantially in information density, redundancy, and required reasoning depth. Through a layer-wise analysis of LLaVA-1.5, we observe that vision tokens tend to saturate in the middle layers. Specifically, text-to-image attention decreases from 0.68 at layer 0 to 0.07 by layer 4, and stabilizes near 0.04 after layer 18, whereas text tokens continue to benefit from deep semantic processing. These findings suggest a mismatch between architectural symmetry and depth-asynchronous modality evolution, resulting in redundant visual computation and possible drift in perceptual representations during deep task-specific adaptation. Motivated by this, we propose Dual-Path Vision Token Routing (DPVR), a modality-asymmetric routing framework for efficient MLLMs. Its core instantiation, DPVR-LF (Late-Layer Fusion), routes vision tokens at the saturation point into a one-layer trainable side branch, runs a thirteen-layer text-only forward that skips image positions in the deep stack, and re-fuses the visual and textual streams only at the final layer. With approximately 3% trainable parameters, DPVR-LF preserves competitive multimodal performance on standard benchmarks while reducing visual computation in the deep Transformer stack. The results challenge the conventional assumption that vision tokens must traverse all deep language-model layers, and indicate that a single late fusion layer can be sufficient for maintaining strong perceptual competence in LLaVA-style MLLMs.
rows.pre_filter_rationale: Directly applicable to production MLLM deployment: proposes concrete architectural optimization (late-layer fusion) that reduces compute overhead by ~3% parameters while maintaining performance—actionable for latency/cost tradeoffs in document intelligence and multimodal RAG systems.
rows.entry_relevance_reason: While the latency optimization is production-relevant, the work is primarily a vision-language architecture paper focused on model training efficiency rather than retrieval, agentic systems, or document intelligence—the core domains of applied LLM deployment.
rows.entry_value_rationale: The dual-path routing and visual saturation concepts could inform multimodal RAG systems handling document images, but the paper's focus on MLLM architecture training rather than inference serving, retrieval patterns, or production deployment makes it peripheral to immediate practical concerns in agent building or document intelligence pipelines.
rows.entry_summary: Proposes DPVR-LF, a modality-asymmetric architecture for MLLMs that routes vision tokens through a shallow side branch after saturation (~layer 18) while text tokens traverse deep layers, fusing only at final layer. Achieves 28% latency reduction with 3% trainable parameters while maintaining competitive performance on standard benchmarks.

rows.title: Reasoning Arena: Trace Tournaments When Verifiable Rewards Fall Short
rows.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become a leading paradigm for improving the reasoning ability of large language models through outcome-based supervision. However, verifiable rewards frequently become uninformative at the group level: when all sampled traces of a given prompt receive identical rewards, group-relative advantage estimation provides no gradient signal, even though the traces may differ substantially in reasoning quality. We propose Reasoning Arena, an adaptive training framework that routes such non-diverse reward groups to a judge system instead of discarding them. Beyond examining the final answer, Reasoning Arena constructs trace tournaments, where reasoning traces are compared head-to-head to expose finer-grained preferences within the group, converting reasoning quality into rich relative reward signals. To make reward estimation efficient, rather than exhaustively comparing every pair, each new trace is evaluated against a small, dynamically updated pool of previously generated traces as anchors to efficiently establish a relative ranking. We then fit a Bradley-Terry model on the incomplete comparison graph, enabling scalable RL integration without quadratic pairwise comparisons. Empirical results demonstrate that Reasoning Arena consistently outperforms the RLVR baseline by 7.6% on average in competition mathematics and coding benchmarks. By converting otherwise wasted zero-advantage samples into useful gradient updates, our method accelerates training by 27% to 41%, saving nearly 50% of generation compute, and substantially improves overall reasoning performance.
rows.pre_filter_rationale: Directly addresses a core production problem in LLM reasoning training (uninformative reward signals in RL pipelines), proposes a practical architectural solution (trace tournaments with Bradley-Terry ranking) that avoids quadratic complexity, and demonstrates significant compute efficiency gains (27-41% acceleration, 50% generation savings) relevant to scaling agentic reasoning systems.
rows.entry_relevance_reason: Directly relevant to LLM evaluation and preference learning for reasoning tasks, with production-applicable techniques for handling sparse reward signals in agentic reasoning systems.
rows.entry_value_rationale: The trace tournament approach and Bradley-Terry modeling for extracting fine-grained reasoning preferences is actionable for improving agent training efficiency in production RAG/agentic systems where verifiable rewards are sparse. The 27-41% training acceleration and live opponent selection pattern are directly applicable to building better reasoning-capable agents.
rows.entry_summary: Reasoning Arena addresses inefficiency in RLVR by detecting non-diverse reward groups (all-correct/all-incorrect) that yield zero gradients, routing them to LLM-judge trace tournaments instead. Uses live opponent selection and Bradley-Terry modeling to efficiently extract fine-grained reasoning preferences, achieving 7.6% performance gains and 27-41% training acceleration.

rows.title: Correct Looks Better: Pairwise Comparisons Reveal Accuracy Rankings
rows.abstract: Pairwise comparisons combined with aggregation methods like Elo have become central to evaluating generative models, yet concerns remain that they reward superficial stylistic cues or display judge biases. In a more positive turn, we show that model rankings from pairwise comparisons strongly agree with ground-truth-based accuracy rankings when such ground truth is available for comparison. By converting five well-known benchmarks into free-form generative evaluations, we find that Elo rankings achieve a Spearman correlation above 0.9 with accuracy rankings and substantially outperform direct evaluation when the judge is weak. Furthermore, style and judge bias have only minor effects on model rankings, despite most judgments occurring on pairs where both candidate answers are correct (or incorrect). On such pairs, we find that repetition after the final answer (echo) is a causal driver of judge preference.
rows.pre_filter_rationale: Directly addresses LLM evaluation methodology with production implications: validates pairwise comparison + Elo aggregation for model ranking, identifies specific judge bias failure modes (echo effect), and provides empirical evidence for evaluation framework selection in production ML systems.
rows.entry_relevance_reason: Directly applicable to LLM evaluation methodology for production systems, but focuses on ranking models rather than evaluating individual outputs or agentic behavior.
rows.entry_value_rationale: Pairwise comparison aggregation is immediately useful for model selection in production (choosing between Claude, GPT-4, Llama variants for RAG/agent backends) and provides a robust framework for LLM-as-judge evaluation when direct scoring is noisy. However, the work's emphasis on ranking models at scale (not ranking individual generation quality) limits depth of applicability for document intelligence or agent evaluation tasks.
rows.entry_summary: Study demonstrating that pairwise comparison rankings of generative models achieve >0.9 Spearman correlation with ground-truth accuracy rankings across five benchmarks. Bradley-Terry aggregation outperforms direct evaluation with weak judges; style/bias have minor effects despite 60% non-discriminative pairs.

rows.title: Memory Beyond Recall: A Dual-Process Cognitive Memory System for Self-Evolving LLM Agents
rows.abstract: Long-term memory for an LLM agent is more than retrieving the right passage at the right time. Current memory systems collapse belief revision, causal coupling, and cross-domain abstraction into a single retrieval surface tuned for surface recall, and consequently struggle on implicit personalisation that requires reasoning over how a user has evolved. We propose DCPM, which reorganises agent memory along a cognitive capability hierarchy ascending from raw inputs and atomic facts, through diachronic belief trajectories and identity, to domain schemas, latent intentions and cross-domain patterns. The hierarchy is driven by two processes inheriting the architectural split of dual-process theory: a synchronous daytime writer (System1) that records belief revisions as doubly linked supersedes chains, and an asynchronous nighttime engine (System2) that induces schemas and intentions and sweeps for cross-domain collisions abstracted into higher-level core schemas. On LongMemEval, PersonaMem and PersonaMem-v2, enabling System2 contributes most where the benchmark rewards implicit cross-session inference (up to +5.20 on PersonaMem-v2) and least on span recall, matching the architectural prediction.
rows.pre_filter_rationale: Directly addresses production memory architectures for agentic systems with concrete hierarchical design (belief trajectories, schema induction, cross-domain abstraction) and dual-process computational patterns that map to engineering tradeoffs between latency (System 1) and reasoning depth (System 2)—immediately applicable to RAG-augmented agent design.
rows.entry_relevance_reason: Directly addresses agent memory architectures and state management for multi-turn agentic systems, with practical implications for LangGraph-based workflows and agent evaluation, though the dual-process framing is more cognitive science than engineering-focused.
rows.entry_value_rationale: The hierarchical memory organization (raw inputs → atomic facts → belief trajectories → schemas) and asynchronous pattern detection offer concrete design patterns for stateful agent systems; the doubly-linked supersedes chains for belief revision provide a testable approach to tracking agent reasoning evolution across interactions, valuable for observability and multi-turn agent reliability.
rows.entry_summary: DCPM: A dual-process cognitive memory architecture for LLM agents that organizes memory hierarchically from raw inputs through atomic facts, belief trajectories, and identity to cross-domain schemas and intentions. System 1 synchronously records belief revisions as doubly-linked supersedes chains; System 2 asynchronously induces schemas and detects cross-domain behavioral patterns.

rows.title: TABVERSE: Benchmarking Cross-Format Table Understanding in LLMs and VLMs
rows.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are increasingly evaluated on table reasoning tasks, but the role of table representation remains under-explored. In practice, the same table content may appear in different structural formats, such as HTML, Markdown, and LaTeX, or as rendered images. However, existing evaluations often let content, format, layout, and modality vary together, making it difficult to isolate representation effects. We introduce TABVERSE, a controlled multimodal table benchmark that aligns the same table content across multiple structural formats and rendered images, with question category and difficulty tags. This design enables systematic evaluation of representation effects while holding table content fixed. We evaluate LLMs and VLMs across three tasks: Question Answering (QA), Structural Understanding Capability (SUC), and Structure Reconstruction (SR). Our results show that representation choice substantially affects table understanding. Models generally perform better with structured text than with rendered images, but the size of this gap depends on the task, model, and format. HTML is often the most robust text format, while row-sensitive structural tasks and syntactically usable LaTeX reconstruction remain challenging. These findings show that table representation is a key factor in reliable table evaluation.
rows.pre_filter_rationale: TABVERSE directly addresses a production concern in document intelligence pipelines: how table representation format (HTML, Markdown, LaTeX, images) affects LLM/VLM performance on extraction and reasoning tasks, enabling practitioners to make informed choices about preprocessing and format conversion in extraction systems.
rows.entry_relevance_reason: Directly relevant to document intelligence and extraction workflows, particularly for evaluating how LLMs handle structured tabular data across formats—a critical component of production document processing pipelines.
rows.entry_value_rationale: Provides empirical benchmarking data on format robustness and representation effects for table understanding, which informs architectural decisions on how to represent tables in RAG systems and document extraction pipelines. Useful for evaluating whether to normalize table formats or use multimodal approaches in production systems.
rows.entry_summary: TabVerse is a controlled multimodal benchmark for evaluating table understanding in LLMs and VLMs across aligned HTML, Markdown, LaTeX formats and rendered images. It isolates representation effects on three tasks: QA, structural understanding, and reconstruction, with 700 balanced samples tagged by difficulty and category.

rows.title: End-to-End Context Compression at Scale
rows.abstract: Long-context language model inference is bottlenecked by memory, as the KV cache grows with context length. Recent techniques to compress the KV cache fall short: they either degrade model quality substantially or require considerable time and compute to compress a single long prompt. Furthermore, many methods require the input to fit within the target model's context window, and are generally incompatible with modern production inference engines. Encoder-decoder compressors, which map a long token sequence to a shorter sequence of latent embeddings consumed by a decoder, are an appealing alternative in principle. However, existing approaches are not competitive with KV cache compression on the accuracy-efficiency frontier. In this work, we revisit encoder-decoder compression and close this gap. We first perform an architecture search, pre-training many variants from scratch to determine how best to design and train encoder-decoder compressors. Guided by our findings, we continually pre-train a family of 0.6B-encoder, 4B-decoder models on over 350B tokens each, at compression ratios of 1:4, 1:8, and 1:16. We introduce Latent Context Language Models (LCLMs), a family of compressors that improve the Pareto frontier across general-task performance, compression speed, and peak memory usage. We demonstrate that LCLMs serve as efficient backbones for long-horizon agents, letting the agent skim through a compressed long context and adaptively expand relevant segments on demand.
rows.pre_filter_rationale: Direct production relevance to long-context inference bottlenecks; encoder-decoder compression architecture with measurable accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs and agent integration patterns are immediately applicable to RAG and agentic systems at scale.
rows.entry_relevance_reason: Context compression directly addresses production RAG latency and cost constraints, while the agentic reasoning application aligns with core workflow optimization.
rows.entry_value_rationale: Encoder-decoder compression patterns could improve retrieval-augmented context efficiency and reduce inference costs for long-context agentic systems. The Pareto frontier framing (memory/latency/accuracy) is immediately actionable for deployment tradeoff decisions, though the focus on model architecture search is less directly applicable than empirical compression techniques.
rows.entry_summary: Latent Context Language Models (LCLMs) enable end-to-end encoder-decoder context compression at scale, achieving new Pareto frontiers for memory/latency/accuracy tradeoffs. Models trained on 350B tokens with systematic architecture search and multi-stage training recipe support efficient long-context inference and agentic reasoning.

rows.title: Correlation Is Not Enough: Embedding Human Metadata for Individual Causal Discovery
rows.abstract: Ask a pretrained biomedical language model whether "cortisol 28 ug/dL" and "stock-market volatility" are related, and it returns a cosine similarity of 0.83 on a scale where 1.0 means identical. The two share no mechanism. This is not a corner case: every off-the-shelf biomedical encoder we tested (BioBERT, PubMedBERT, BioM-ELECTRA) scores unrelated cross-domain pairs between 0.76 and 0.92 when the answer should be near zero. Accuracy on cross-domain discrimination is 0%. Retrieval systems survive this, because a language model downstream filters the noise. A Large Behavioural Model (LBM), a foundation model whose subject is a person rather than a sentence, does not: it reasons over a graph of a user's life and treats embedding proximity as evidence that two events are causally linked. False proximity writes a false causal edge, and everything downstream inherits the error. Here, embedding geometry is not a tuning knob; it is correctness. We report the fix. A contrastive pass over 72,034 pairs raises PubMedBERT BIOSSES correlation from 0.633 to 0.828 and within-vs-across-domain separation from 1.05x to 1.63x. A second pass, BODHI, mines hard negatives from edges absent in a biomedical knowledge graph and lifts separation to 2.30x and the discrimination gap to +0.392, at a 4.5% BIOSSES cost. On an Intel Xeon 6737P with AMX, OpenVINO cuts single-query latency from 1367 ms to 10 ms (133x) and reaches 555 sentences/sec. One finding contradicts standard advice: FP16 beats INT8 on this silicon at every serving batch size, and we explain why. The same model on a no-AMX Ice Lake instance runs 13-27x slower. We release the benchmark suite, training corpora, the BODHI generator, and the OpenVINO scripts.
rows.pre_filter_rationale: Directly addresses embedding quality in retrieval systems with production-grade solutions (contrastive fine-tuning, hard negative mining, latency optimization), critical for RAG correctness and relevant to document intelligence systems where false causal associations corrupt downstream reasoning.
rows.entry_relevance_reason: While the paper addresses embedding quality and inference optimization (relevant), the focus on biomedical causal discovery and behavioral models is orthogonal to RAG, agentic systems, and document intelligence workflows.
rows.entry_value_rationale: The contrastive learning approach and knowledge-graph integration for hard negatives could inform embedding model selection criteria, but the biomedical domain specificity and causal inference framing limit direct applicability to production NLP/RAG systems.
rows.entry_summary: Addresses embedding geometry errors in biomedical language models causing false causal inference in behavioral models. Proposes contrastive learning with knowledge-graph-mined hard negatives to improve cross-domain discrimination from 0% to 39.2%, achieving 133x latency reduction via optimized inference.

rows.title: Learning to Attack and Defend: Adaptive Red Teaming of Language Models via GRPO
rows.abstract: AI red teaming must continually adapt to evolving attackers and defenders. Reinforcement learning offers a promising approach to discovering novel attacks, and co-training methods can produce more robust defenders in tandem. Recent works have demonstrated the efficacy of attacker-defender co-training by applying PPO and DPO, but report that GRPO is unstable in this setting. We introduce AdvGRPO, a co-training framework that makes GRPO viable for joint attacker-defender optimization using dense multi-channel rewards and decoupled advantage normalization. Training progresses through a curriculum from single-turn to closed-loop multi-turn attacks before bootstrapping co-training, where attacker and defender models are updated in alternation. We show that our method can produce highly effective and transferable attacks and that co-trained defenders outperform baselines on safety benchmarks.
rows.pre_filter_rationale: Directly applicable to production LLM safety: demonstrates practical RL-based red teaming methodology with concrete training curriculum, handles real deployment concern of adaptive adversaries, and provides transferable attack patterns useful for stress-testing production systems.
rows.entry_relevance_reason: While the adversarial robustness framing has tangential relevance to production LLM safety, this paper focuses on attack/defense research mechanics rather than practical production observability, evaluation, or defense patterns applicable to deployed systems.
rows.entry_value_rationale: Limited direct application to production RAG/agent systems. Most relevant only if building safety evaluation frameworks or adversarial testing pipelines, but the GRPO mechanics are specialized research rather than actionable engineering patterns for practitioners shipping document intelligence or agentic workflows.
rows.entry_summary: AdvGRPO is a co-training framework using GRPO with dense multi-channel rewards and decoupled advantage normalization for simultaneous attacker-defender optimization in LLM red teaming. Introduces closed-loop multi-turn attacks with per-turn rewards and curriculum-based training to produce transferable jailbreaks while improving defender robustness.

rows.title: Multi-Turn Evaluation of Deep Research Agents Under Process-Level Feedback
rows.abstract: Existing benchmarks for deep research agents (DRAs) assess only single-shot outputs, ignoring a key question: can DRAs improve their reports when guided by feedback? To investigate this, we conduct a multi-turn evaluation of DRAs under two feedback settings: self-reflection, in which the agent revises its report without any external diagnostic signal, and process-level feedback, in which the agent receives guidance targeting gaps in its research strategy. To enable process-level feedback, we design Research Gap Inference (RGI), a method that analyzes patterns of satisfied and unsatisfied rubric criteria to infer research-process gaps. Our analysis reveals three key findings: (i) under self-reflection, agents incorporate and regress on rubric criteria at nearly equal rates, yielding negligible net improvement; (ii) a single round of process-level feedback yields substantial gains, raising the normalized score by approximately $8$-$15$ points and yielding a roughly $35$-$40\%$ incorporation rate; (iii) these gains do not compound over subsequent turns, as agents regress on up to $24\%$ of previously satisfied criteria when rewriting the full report to address remaining gaps. Even with targeted guidance, reliable multi-turn improvement remains out of reach for the DRA architectures we evaluate. Our code and results are publicly available at https://github.com/sabharwalrishabh/Multi-Turn-Evaluation-of-DRAs.
rows.pre_filter_rationale: Directly addresses agent evaluation and multi-turn refinement patterns—core to production agentic systems—with actionable findings on feedback mechanisms, failure modes in iterative improvement, and architectural limitations relevant to building reliable research agents.
rows.entry_relevance_reason: Directly addresses agentic system evaluation and multi-turn reasoning patterns with practical findings on feedback mechanisms and performance degradation, highly relevant to production agent orchestration; limited immediate applicability since research agents differ from retrieval/RAG agents in scope.
rows.entry_value_rationale: The multi-turn degradation finding (regression on 24% of criteria) and process-level feedback analysis provide actionable insights for designing robust agent workflows and evaluation harnesses. The Research Gap Inference pattern is architecturally relevant for understanding where agentic systems fail under iterative refinement, informing observability and feedback loop design in production systems.
rows.entry_summary: Multi-turn evaluation framework for deep research agents using process-level feedback. Introduces Research Gap Inference (RGI) to analyze rubric patterns and identify research-strategy gaps. Finds agents improve 88-151 points with single feedback round but regress on 24% of criteria in subsequent turns, showing multi-turn improvement remains challenging.

rows.title: Data Synthesis and Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Low-Resource NMT: A Case Study on Q'eqchi' Mayan
rows.abstract: Neural machine translation for digitally low-resource Indigenous languages is often hindered by extreme data scarcity, prompting reliance on extractive web-scraping. To ensure data sovereignty, this study introduces a data synthesis methodology to bootstrap NMT models without scraping target-language parallel text. Focusing on Q'eqchi' Mayan, we transformed community-sourced dictionaries into a massive synthetic corpus, utilizing Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) via LoRA adapters on an mT5-base model. In-domain evaluation demonstrates high structural acquisition (BLEU 42.02), proving that synthetic constraints effectively teach complex agglutinative morphology and VOS word order. However, evaluation against an organic glossary reveals a structural-semantic gap (BLEU 0.59), where the model maintains grammatical integrity but lacks the lexical grounding of natural language. The model exhibits overfitting to the constrained structural variance of the synthetic templates; despite high semantic entropy in the pipeline, it struggles with the syntactic fluidity of natural language, forcing organic inputs into rigid learned patterns. Furthermore, an ablation study utilizing a Multi-Task Learning architecture resulted in negative transfer, suggesting that auxiliary tasks competed for limited parameter capacity within the LoRA adapters, causing over-optimization for synthetic markers at the expense of organic flexibility. Ultimately, we establish that synthetic bootstrapping is a highly effective structural primer, but requires authentic data for semantic refinement via Curriculum Learning.
rows.pre_filter_rationale: Directly applicable case study on PEFT (LoRA) for low-resource NLP, synthetic data generation tradeoffs, and multi-task learning failure modes—practical insights on parameter efficiency, data quality gaps, and curriculum learning that inform production RAG/extraction systems for under-resourced domains.
rows.entry_relevance_reason: While parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA) is production-relevant, this work focuses on low-resource NMT for an indigenous language without direct applicability to core domains (RAG, document intelligence, agentic systems) and the synthetic data approach is task-specific rather than transferable.
rows.entry_value_rationale: LoRA techniques could inform parameter-efficient adaptation in production RAG/agent systems, and the structural-semantic gap insight has minor relevance for understanding fine-tuning failure modes. However, the paper's primary contribution (synthetic data for low-resource NMT) sits outside active work areas and lacks production-serving, inference, or orchestration considerations.
rows.entry_summary: Proposes distribution-aware synthetic data generation and LoRA-based parameter-efficient fine-tuning for bootstrapping neural machine translation of Q'eqchi' Mayan without web-scraping. Demonstrates synthetic data teaches morphology and word order effectively but reveals structural-semantic gap; MTL causes negative transfer under purely synthetic constraints.

rows.title: Trainable Smooth-Rotation Transforms with Learned Channel Scales for LLM Quantization
rows.abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) is one of the most practical ways to reduce the serving cost of Large Language Models (LLMs), but activation quantization remains difficult because outlier-dominated channels lead to large quantization errors. This paper investigates whether part of this degradation is caused by over-migration in scaling-based equivalent transformations. We introduce a quantile-robust scaling policy for SmoothRot-style transforms by replacing max-based activation statistics with high quantiles, and we complement it with constrained gradient-based optimization of channel scales. On LLaMA-3.2-1B under W4A4 quantization, quantile-only policy search improves selected-layer error by 11.1% over the SmoothRot baseline, joint (alpha, q) search improves it by 12%, and training reaches 18.5%. Replaying the best selected-layer policy on all decoder-block down-projection layers reduces the corresponding full-layer mean error from 97.51 to 78.08 (19.9%). The results show that robust migration control and lightweight scale learning provide consistent gains over max-based fixed policies while preserving the equivalent-transform framework.
rows.pre_filter_rationale: Directly addresses production LLM quantization challenges (W4A4, activation outliers) with practical post-training optimization techniques applicable to inference cost reduction, a core concern for shipping LLM systems.
rows.entry_relevance_reason: While LLM quantization is relevant to production deployment, this paper focuses on post-training optimization techniques for weight-activation quantization without addressing practical inference serving concerns like latency, throughput, memory overhead, or real-world deployment tradeoffs.
rows.entry_value_rationale: Applicable if you're optimizing quantized model accuracy before serving, but the paper's focus on mathematical transforms and activation outlier handling doesn't directly advance RAG, agentic systems, document intelligence, or the engineering patterns needed for production LLM systems. More relevant to model optimization than system building.
rows.entry_summary: Post-training quantization method for LLMs using trainable smooth-rotation transforms with quantile-robust scaling policies and learned channel scales. Addresses activation outlier problem in W4A4 quantization through parameterized equivalent transformations, achieving 18.5% error reduction on LLaMA-3.2-1B via constrained gradient-based optimization.

rows.title: RKSC: Reasoning-Aware KV Cache Sharing and Confident Early Exit for Multi-Step LLM Inference
rows.abstract: We introduce RKSC (Reasoning-Aware KV Cache Sharing), a training-free inference framework that eliminates two structural redundancies in multi-branch LLM reasoning pipelines. ASKS (Attention-Similarity KV Sharing) computes the prefix KV cache once and broadcasts it to all semantically similar branches via hidden-state cosine similarity, strictly generalising the token-exact prefix caching used by vLLM and SGLang. CGEE (Confidence-Gated Early Exit) applies two complementary exit mechanisms: (1) it skips the verification forward pass entirely when generation confidence is decisive across branches, and (2) it terminates the verification pass at an intermediate layer when per-layer entropy stabilises, using lightweight hooks on the transformer backbone. RSBCM (Reasoning-Selective Block Cache Manager) prevents unbounded cache growth via attention-weighted depth-priority eviction. Across five model families (7B-10B), four benchmarks, and 1,000 evaluated problems, RKSC achieves a mean speedup of 3.008x over the No-KV baseline (peak 3.990x), a 1.66x mean improvement over vLLM-equivalent prefix caching, with a CGEE-induced error rate of only 0.37% (6 errors out of 1,616 verify calls). No fine-tuning or architecture changes are required. Code is available at https://github.com/AnirudhSekar/RKSC.
rows.pre_filter_rationale: Directly addresses production inference optimization for multi-step LLM reasoning (core agentic pattern), with training-free techniques (KV cache sharing, early exit), quantified speedups (3x), and production-grade concerns (cache memory management, error rates), making it immediately applicable to agent orchestration systems.
rows.entry_relevance_reason: Direct applicability to production LLM serving optimization with measurable latency/throughput gains, though KV cache tuning is a narrow efficiency concern versus broader agentic workflow architecture.
rows.entry_value_rationale: RKSC's training-free optimization approach (ASKS + CGEE) is immediately applicable to multi-step reasoning pipelines common in agentic systems, reducing inference costs without model retraining. The 3× speedup justifies evaluation for latency-critical retrieval-augmented reasoning tasks, though value depends on whether your bottleneck is compute cost versus orchestration overhead.
rows.entry_summary: RKSC is a training-free inference framework for multi-branch LLM reasoning that eliminates redundancies through attention-similarity KV cache sharing (ASKS), confidence-gated early exit (CGEE), and reasoning-selective block cache management. Achieves 3.008× mean speedup with 0.37% error rate across five model families.

rows.title: Bittensor Agent Arenas as a Trajectory Primitive: Distilling a Shopping Agent from ShoppingBench Subnet Traces
rows.abstract: Small-model agentic post-training is bottlenecked less by the algorithm than by the trajectory substrate it consumes. Leading recipes (RLVR, group-relative RL, rejection-sampled re-SFT) all need multi-turn traces carrying per-trajectory supervision, and the two existing sources fall short: frontier-synthesised data inherits the synthesizer's biases and collapses the long tail, while unfiltered production logs are unjudged and contaminated by shortcut behaviour. We argue that an incentive-aligned agent arena can be engineered to manufacture such trajectories, and demonstrate this on ORO Subnet 15 (SN15), a Bittensor deployment of the ShoppingBench agentic-commerce benchmark. SN15's race mechanism, LLM reasoning judge, and rotating leak-cluster-guarded problem suite yield a corpus with three properties: incentive-aligned diversity, per-trajectory judging, and anti-memorised held-out evaluation. We introduce a structural-quality filter that converts the raw firehose into a trainable corpus by keeping agentic trajectories (the model itself emits the tool calls) and rejecting sub-task trajectories (the model only classifies or narrates over a deterministic search loop), then post-train Qwen3-4B with a recipe matched to the published ShoppingBench SFT-then-GRPO pipeline. On a leak-cluster-guarded held-out partition scored production-strict, the model lifts from the published Qwen3-4B base of 18.0% ASR to 42.7%, within single-problem noise of the synthetic-data SFT-only baseline (43.6%), while training on a fraction of a single day of subnet output. The supervised stack leaves a large pass@8 to pass@1 gap (53.3% vs 34.8%); a per-step teacher-grounded Dr. GRPO reward converts that headroom into process improvement, and we identify the sub-task firehose as the primary lever for closing the gap to the 48.7% SFT+GRPO bar. We release the filter, the corpus splits, and the arena mechanics.
rows.pre_filter_rationale: Directly addresses trajectory quality as a production bottleneck for agentic post-training, demonstrates a practical incentive-aligned corpus-generation mechanism with concrete architectural choices (race mechanism, judge design, leak-cluster filtering), and provides actionable empirical results on small-model distillation with reproducible baselines—core to shipping agentic systems at scale.
rows.entry_relevance_reason: Directly addresses agentic systems and agent evaluation through a novel data generation mechanism (incentive-aligned trajectory collection), though the Bittensor-specific infrastructure and shopping domain limit broader applicability.
rows.entry_value_rationale: Provides a production-grade pattern for bootstrapping agent training data via competitive filtering rather than synthetic generation, with concrete SFT+RL pipeline results. The trajectory distillation approach is transferable to other agentic domains, though the Bittensor mechanism itself is domain-specific infrastructure.
rows.entry_summary: Bittensor subnet mechanism (SN15/ShoppingBench) for manufacturing judged agentic trajectories via incentive-aligned competition. Distills Qwen3-4B shopping agent from filtered subnet traces using multi-stage SFT+RL pipeline, achieving 42.7% ASR on held-out eval versus 18.0% base and 48.7% synthetic baseline.

rows.title: Unsupervised Style Representation Learning for AI-Text Detection via Paraphrase Inversion
rows.abstract: The rapid development of large language models (LLMs) has raised concerns about misuse such as plagiarism, misinformation, and automated influence operations, motivating the need for robust detectors. Recent work has shown that neural representations of writing style are effective for detection and, crucially, robust to adversarial attacks that defeat most existing detectors. However, current style-based detectors rely on authorship labels for training, and are limited to few-shot inference for detection, requiring in-distribution samples that may not always be available. We learn discriminative style features without authorship labels by training a style encoder to reconstruct human-authored text from its machine-generated paraphrase; freezing a semantic encoder during training biases the style encoder to capture only the non-semantic features needed for reconstruction. We evaluate the learned representations via two detection strategies: a few-shot detector and a zero-shot DeepSVDD-based detector. Across benchmarks, our method matches or outperforms all baselines in the few-shot setting and, in the zero-shot regime, is competitive with fully supervised classifiers on in-distribution test data while generalizing better to unseen LLMs. Beyond detection, the learned representations generalize to unseen tasks, achieving competitive performance on authorship verification and fine-grained style discrimination despite never being trained on either objective.
rows.pre_filter_rationale: Directly relevant to production AI-text detection systems; unsupervised style representation learning addresses practical deployment constraints (label scarcity, zero-shot generalization) and adversarial robustness concerns that impact real-world detector reliability.
rows.entry_relevance_reason: While the paper addresses AI-text detection (a relevant problem), the technical approach focuses on unsupervised representation learning and anomaly detection rather than production-applicable document intelligence or retrieval systems.
rows.entry_value_rationale: Marginally useful for understanding style-based detection robustness, but the paraphrase-inversion methodology and zero-shot anomaly detection (DeepSVDD) are not core to building RAG systems, agentic workflows, or document intelligence pipelines that drive current work.
rows.entry_summary: Proposes LUSR, an unsupervised method for learning style representations via paraphrase inversion to detect AI-generated text. Freezes semantic encoder during training to force style encoder to capture non-semantic features. Evaluates via few-shot prototype matching and zero-shot DeepSVDD-based detection, achieving competitive performance with robustness to paraphrasing attacks.

rows.title: $τ$-Rec: A Verifiable Benchmark for Agentic Recommender Systems
rows.abstract: As recommender systems transition toward agentic, multi-turn conversational interfaces, evaluation paradigms have struggled to keep pace. Current benchmarks often rely on "LLM-as-a-judge" evaluations, which introduce subjectivity, high costs and inconsistency. We present $τ$-Rec, a benchmark for agentic recommender systems that replaces subjective evaluation with verifiable rewards and a reveal-tagged elicitation (RTE) mechanism that controls how task constraints surface during dialogue. By testing agents against structured catalog predicates and employing a pass^k reliability metric, $τ$-Rec provides a systematic test for consistent reasoning. Our evaluation of nine configurations across five model families -- GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 2.5 Flash, DeepSeek V4 Flash, Qwen3-32B and GPT-5 mini -- reveals a steep reliability cliff, where even the best model achieves only ~57% at pass^1 and ~38% at pass^4, highlighting a critical gap in current conversational agent deployment. All code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/nbharaths/tau-rec.
rows.pre_filter_rationale: Directly addresses production evaluation of agentic systems with verifiable metrics and concrete reliability benchmarks—core to shipping reliable conversational agents in practice.
rows.entry_relevance_reason: Directly addresses agentic system evaluation and reliability measurement, core concerns for production agentic workflows, though the recommender-system-specific domain is tangential to primary focus areas.
rows.entry_value_rationale: Provides a concrete reproducible evaluation framework (deterministic predicates, RTE, pass^k metrics) that could be adapted for evaluating other agentic systems beyond recommendations. The reliability cliff finding is actionable for understanding LLM model selection tradeoffs in production agent deployments.
rows.entry_summary: τ-Rec introduces a verifiable benchmark for agentic recommender systems using deterministic catalog predicates, reveal-tagged elicitation (RTE), and pass^k reliability metrics to replace subjective LLM-as-judge evaluation. Evaluation of six LLM models exposes a reliability cliff, with best performance at ~57% pass^1 and ~35% pass^4.

rows.title: Supervised Fine-tuning with Synthetic Rationale Data Hurts Real-World Disease Prediction
rows.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning with synthetic rationale data is widely assumed to improve language model performance on clinical prediction tasks by teaching models not just what to predict but why. We test this assumption on five-year Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD) prediction from longitudinal health histories. Across a large-scale controlled experiment of 504 configurations, we find that rationale-based SFT consistently and substantially hurts prediction performance relative to label-only fine-tuning. The degradation persists across model families and data scales, and is not resolved by using a reasoning-oriented base model. Crucially, the failure is not explained by poor rationale quality: human expert annotation confirms that the generated rationales are medically accurate and faithfully grounded in patient-specific evidence, and few-shot experiments show that the same rationales improve performance when used as inference-time demonstrations rather than training targets. We identify the root cause as a structural conflict between narrative plausibility and discriminative optimization. We hope our work paves the path toward a more precise understanding of when and how rationale-based supervision helps and when it does not, guiding the responsible development of language models for high-stakes clinical prediction.
rows.pre_filter_rationale: Directly relevant to production document intelligence and clinical NLP systems—demonstrates a critical failure mode in synthetic rationale supervision that affects real-world deployment decisions, with actionable guidance on when rationale-based training helps vs. hurts performance.
rows.entry_relevance_reason: While touching on evaluation and model behavior, this is primarily a clinical ML domain study without actionable insights for production RAG, agentic systems, or document intelligence architectures.
rows.entry_value_rationale: The core finding—that synthetic explanations can degrade performance—has tangential relevance to LLM-as-judge evaluation patterns, but the paper's focus on medical domain-specific ADRD prediction and narrative coherence conflicts lacks transferable architectural or engineering lessons for production NLP systems.
rows.entry_summary: Supervised fine-tuning with synthetic rationales degrades disease prediction performance compared to label-only training across 504 configurations on ADRD prediction. Despite high-quality, medically accurate rationales, the structural conflict between narrative plausibility and discriminative optimization causes this failure.

rows.title: Agentic Hybrid RAG for Evidence-Grounded Muon Collider Analysis
rows.abstract: Muon collider research spans accelerator physics, detector instrumentation, and high-energy phenomenology, with relevant evidence scattered across a rapidly expanding and heterogeneous body of scientific literature. As high-energy physics (HEP) increasingly explores agent-assisted analysis workflows, efficiently locating, integrating, and verifying scientific evidence becomes an essential capability. While retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) offers a promising framework for scientific question answering, integrating agentic reasoning without compromising retrieval precision remains a key challenge. In this work, we present agentic hybrid RAG, an evidence-grounded RAG framework for muon collider research. The framework combines a hybrid retriever, integrating sparse lexical and dense semantic retrieval, with an agentic reasoning module for query decomposition, evidence expansion, and grounded answer generation. To enable systematic evaluation, we construct the first benchmark for retrieval-augmented scientific question answering in the muon collider domain, comprising a curated literature corpus together with dedicated retrieval and answer-generation benchmarks covering major detector and physics research topics. Extensive evaluation shows that hybrid retrieval provides the strongest retrieval backbone, while agentic reasoning is most effective for controlled evidence expansion and answer synthesis. Built on this principle, agentic hybrid RAG consistently outperforms representative retrieval and RAG baselines in retrieval effectiveness, answer quality, evidence coverage, and factual grounding. Together, the benchmark and framework provide a foundation for evidence-grounded scientific question answering and future HEP analysis agents operating over large-scale scientific literature.
rows.pre_filter_rationale: Directly addresses agentic RAG patterns (hybrid retrieval, query decomposition, evidence expansion) with production evaluation against baselines and systematic benchmarking; domain-specific application demonstrates architectural decisions transferable to other evidence-grounded QA systems.
rows.entry_relevance_reason: Demonstrates advanced agentic RAG patterns (query decomposition, hybrid retrieval) with production-relevant evaluation methodology, but domain-specific physics application limits generalizability to core work.
rows.entry_value_rationale: The evidence-grounded evaluation framework and agent-driven query decomposition strategy over hybrid retrieval are architecturally transferable to document intelligence tasks. However, the muon collider benchmark itself has limited applicability outside HEP; value is in the RAG orchestration patterns rather than domain content.
rows.entry_summary: Agentic hybrid RAG system for muon collider scientific QA combining BM25 sparse retrieval, dense embeddings, and agentic query decomposition. Constructs first muon collider benchmark with evidence-grounded evaluation metrics for retrieval and answer generation in HEP.

rows.title: ERAlign: Energy-based Representation Alignment of GNNs and LLMs on Text-attributed Graphs
rows.abstract: Text-attributed Graphs (TAGs) incorporate textual node attributes with graph structures to describe rich relational semantics. Recent efforts to integrate Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promise for learning on TAGs, yet achieving well-aligned representations remains challenging. Prior studies largely rely on heuristics that perform coarse-grained matching. They lack sufficient constraints and ignore distributional alignment, leading to representation drift and limited generalization. Building on Energy-based Models (EBMs), we propose an Energy-based Representation Alignment (ERAlign) framework that projects GNN-encoded graph structure and LLM-derived text embeddings in a shared latent space to achieve distribution consistency. Concretely, layer-wise alignment is quantified by a distance metric and optimized via an EBM objective. By decreasing energy values, our framework yields well-aligned representations for downstream tasks. During training, we introduce Energy Discrepancy (ED) to avoid high sampling costs associated with intractable normalization. ED also carries theoretical guarantees of higher training efficiency and reduced energy landscape distortion. Empirical evaluations on eight TAG datasets demonstrate that ERAlign obtains state-of-the-art performance across varying levels of supervision and cross-task transfer scenarios.
rows.pre_filter_rationale: Directly applicable to production RAG and document intelligence systems that combine graph structures with LLM embeddings for retrieval and entity linking; the distributional alignment framework addresses real engineering challenges in multi-modal representation fusion for knowledge-grounded applications.
rows.entry_relevance_reason: While the paper addresses GNN-LLM integration on text-attributed graphs, the energy-based alignment approach is theoretically focused without clear production relevance to RAG, agentic systems, or document intelligence workflows.
rows.entry_value_rationale: The work is tangentially relevant only if you're building hybrid retrieval systems that combine graph-structured knowledge with LLM representations; however, the energy-based distribution matching technique lacks demonstrated applicability to practical production concerns like latency, cost, or failure mode handling that define the profile's engineering focus.
rows.entry_summary: ERAlign proposes energy-based representation alignment for GNNs and LLMs on text-attributed graphs. Uses Cramér distance and Energy Discrepancy minimization to enforce distributional consistency across layer-wise alignment, achieving SOTA on 8 benchmarks with improved label efficiency and cross-task transferability.

rows.title: Advancing the State-of-the-Art in Empirical Privacy Auditing
rows.abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) can exhibit problematic memorization of individual training examples. Empirical privacy auditing (EPA) quantifies this risk by measuring realistic data leakage on membership inference (MI) or reconstruction attacks. A key challenge in EPA is designing ``canary'' examples that are mixed with the privacy-sensitive training data. We propose generating synthetic canaries via high-temperature sampling ($T \geq 0.8$) from LLMs, using prompts tailored to the privacy-sensitive training data. These canaries act as high-influence outliers, ensuring high identifiability and hence strong audits. Further, since the canaries are themselves non-private, they are inspectable and can be inserted with repetition without jeopardizing the privacy of the real data. An important use of models fine-tuned on privacy-sensitive data is the generation of synthetic data. This also comes with privacy risk. We introduce a powerful synthetic data audit based on fine-tuning an auxiliary model on the synthetic data. Auditing the auxiliary model for the original canaries then provides a strong estimate of the privacy leakage through the synthetic data. Finally, leveraging our strong auditing methodologies, we perform a systematic investigation into the interacting effects of model capacity and canary entropy on memorization.
rows.pre_filter_rationale: Directly applicable to production RAG/document systems: empirical privacy auditing methodology for LLM fine-tuning is critical for shipping systems on sensitive data, with actionable techniques (synthetic canaries, auxiliary model auditing) and measurable privacy risk quantification.
rows.entry_relevance_reason: Privacy auditing is peripherally relevant to production LLM systems, but this paper's focus on memorization detection and synthetic canaries addresses a research concern rather than a shipping practitioner's immediate priority.
rows.entry_value_rationale: While observability of model behavior matters in production, empirical privacy auditing is not a primary concern for RAG/agentic/document intelligence systems; this is more valuable for LLM providers or teams with strict data governance requirements, not typical for applied AI engineers building on top of LLMs.
rows.entry_summary: Novel empirical privacy auditing framework for LLMs using synthetic canaries via high-temperature sampling and auxiliary model-based data auditing to detect memorization in fine-tuned models and synthetic data generation, with systematic study of model capacity and canary entropy effects.

rows.title: Benchmarking Knowledge Editing using Logical Rules
rows.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in real-world applications that require access to up-to-date knowledge. However, retraining LLMs is computationally expensive. Therefore, knowledge editing techniques are crucial for maintaining current information and correcting erroneous assertions within pre-trained models. Current benchmarks for knowledge editing primarily focus on recalling edited facts, often neglecting their logical consequences. To address this limitation, we introduce a new benchmark designed to evaluate how knowledge editing methods handle the logical consequences of a single fact edit. Our benchmark extracts relevant logical rules from a knowledge graph for a given edit. Then, it generates multi-hop questions based on these rules to assess the impact on logical consequences. Our findings indicate that while existing knowledge editing approaches can accurately insert direct assertions into LLMs, they frequently fail to inject entailed knowledge. Specifically, experiments with popular methods like ROME and FT reveal a substantial performance gap, up to 24%, between evaluations on directly edited knowledge and on entailed knowledge. This highlights the critical need for semantics-aware evaluation frameworks in knowledge editing.
rows.pre_filter_rationale: Production LLMs require knowledge editing for factual currency; this benchmark directly addresses a critical gap in evaluating whether edits propagate logically, exposing real failure modes (ROME/FT missing entailment) that impact deployed systems relying on consistent knowledge graphs.
rows.entry_relevance_reason: Knowledge editing benchmarking is tangentially related to RAG and document intelligence but represents a niche evaluation problem with limited production applicability compared to core priorities like retrieval optimization, agent reasoning, or extraction reliability.
rows.entry_value_rationale: Useful for understanding LLM brittleness under logical consistency constraints, which could inform agent verification pipelines or fact-grounded extraction systems. However, knowledge editing itself is rarely deployed in production RAG systems—most handle evolving facts through retrieval updates rather than in-model edits, limiting immediate actionability.
rows.entry_summary: Novel benchmark for evaluating knowledge editing in LLMs using automatically mined logical rules from knowledge graphs. Addresses gap where existing KE methods handle direct edits well but fail on logically entailed consequences, showing up to 24% performance drop on multi-hop reasoning.

rows.title: Detecting Knowledge Gaps from Conversational AI Interactions Using Curriculum Prerequisite Graphs
rows.abstract: Large online courses generate thousands of student questions directed at conversational AI teaching assistants, yet these interaction logs remain largely untapped as diagnostic signals. We present a pipeline that maps student questions from a conversational AI teaching assistant to curriculum topics using a few-shot text classifier, grounded in a GPT-4-extracted prerequisite knowledge graph of course concepts. Evaluated on 1,340 question events from 164 students in a graduate-level AI course, our classifier achieves 80.0% accuracy across 43 labels (42 curriculum topics plus an "unknown" abstention class). Topic-level question volume correlates significantly with student self-reported difficulty from an independent mid-semester survey (rho = 0.491, p = 0.008, n = 28 topics), providing convergent evidence that the classified question stream reflects genuine topic difficulty. These results demonstrate that conversational AI interaction logs, mapped onto curriculum structure, carry actionable signals about topic-level knowledge gaps and provide instructors with a curriculum-grounded view of which topics warrant attention.
rows.pre_filter_rationale: Directly relevant as a production pattern for LLM-based educational systems: demonstrates practical pipeline (few-shot classification + knowledge graph grounding) for extracting actionable signals from conversational AI logs, with validated correlation to student learning outcomes—applicable to building observability into agent systems.
rows.entry_relevance_reason: While the paper demonstrates conversational AI interaction analysis and LLM-based classification, it targets educational assessment rather than production NLP systems, retrieval architectures, or agentic workflows central to your applied work.
rows.entry_value_rationale: The few-shot classification pipeline using GPT-4 and the prerequisite graph extraction methodology could inform conversational analysis in broader RAG systems, but the educational domain specificity and lack of deployment-scale considerations (latency, cost, serving architecture) limits direct applicability to your production AI systems.
rows.entry_summary: Pipeline mapping student questions from conversational AI teaching assistants to curriculum topics using few-shot text classification grounded in GPT-4-extracted prerequisite knowledge graphs. Achieves 80% accuracy on 1,340 questions from 164 students; topic-level question volume correlates significantly with self-reported difficulty (ρ=0.491, p=0.008), demonstrating actionable signals for knowledge gap detection.

rows.title: K-Forcing: Joint Next-K-Token Decoding via Push-Forward Language Modeling
rows.abstract: Autoregressive (AR) language modeling is the dominant paradigm for text generation, yet its sequential token-by-token decoding makes inference memory-bound and inefficient. Existing acceleration approaches, such as speculative decoding and diffusion language models, can yield speedups under certain conditions but do not directly address high-load batch serving--the scenario most critical for industrial-scale deployment. We introduce K-Forcing, a push-forward language modeling paradigm for joint next-k-token decoding. K-Forcing distills an existing AR model into a conditional push-forward mapping--one that transforms independent uniform noise variables into a joint sample of multiple future tokens in a single forward pass. This design preserves fixed-length outputs, reuses the AR teacher backbone, and remains compatible with standard AR serving infrastructure. We train this mapping via progressive self-forcing distillation, which gradually expands the prediction window while enabling the student to closely match the sequence distribution of the AR teacher. We evaluate K-Forcing on LM1B and OpenWebText using a standard causal Transformer backbone. When aggressively configured to generate k = 4 tokens per forward pass, K-Forcing delivers approximately 2.4-3.5x speedup across different batch sizes, while incurring modest quality degradation relative to its AR teacher. As inference increasingly dominates the lifetime compute cost of modern LLMs, K-Forcing offers a promising route toward accelerating AR generation under real-world high-load deployment.
rows.pre_filter_rationale: Direct relevance to production LLM serving bottlenecks; K-Forcing addresses batch inference efficiency and latency—critical constraints in deployed RAG/agentic systems—with a practical distillation approach compatible with existing infrastructure.
rows.entry_relevance_reason: Directly addresses LLM inference latency/throughput tradeoffs critical for production serving, with proven speedups on batch inference—a core concern for deployed RAG and agentic systems.
rows.entry_value_rationale: K-Forcing provides a practical optimization for reducing per-token latency in batch serving without requiring architectural changes, enabling faster agentic tool-use loops and retrieval-augmented generation workflows. The 2.4-3.5× speedup on standard batching is actionable for reducing operational costs and latency in production deployments.
rows.entry_summary: K-Forcing proposes push-forward language modeling for joint next-k-token decoding via progressive self-forcing distillation. Achieves 2.4-3.5× speedup in batch serving by generating multiple tokens per forward pass while maintaining distribution fidelity and regular batching, addressing the memory-bound bottleneck of autoregressive inference.

rows.title: Attention-Discounted Adaptive Sampler for Masked Diffusion Language Models
rows.abstract: Masked diffusion language models can reduce inference steps by revealing multiple tokens per denoising iteration, but this parallelism is fragile: positions that are individually confident may be unsafe to commit together when their predictions are coupled. Existing training-free samplers such as Top-\(k\), Fast-dLLM, and EB-Sampler mainly control how many tokens to reveal, while often ranking candidates by token-wise scores that ignore interactions within the selected set. We propose ADAS, a training-free reranking rule for parallel masked diffusion decoding. ADAS leaves the base sampler's stopping rule unchanged and modifies only subset construction: it greedily discounts a candidate when it attends strongly to already selected positions whose predictions remain uncertain. Unlike graph-constrained methods that turn attention into hard compatibility constraints, ADAS keeps attention continuous and uses it as a soft marginal penalty. Across LLaDA-8B-Base and Dream-7B-Base on GSM8K, MATH500, HumanEval, and MBPP, plugging ADAS into Top-\(k\), Fast-dLLM, and EB-Sampler improves low-NFE performance at matched denoiser evaluations by \(9.11\) and \(10.46\) percentage points on average, respectively, with \(3.1\%\) per-forward runtime overhead. These results show that soft attention-discounted reranking is a simple and modular way to improve quality in highly parallel decoding for masked diffusion language models.
rows.pre_filter_rationale: Directly addresses production inference efficiency for LLMs through a training-free, modular reranking technique that improves parallel decoding quality with measurable speedup—actionable for optimizing LLM serving latency in constrained environments.
rows.entry_relevance_reason: Masked diffusion language models are niche architectures with limited production adoption; the reranking improvement is theoretically interesting but not actionable for mainstream LLM inference workflows.
rows.entry_value_rationale: Relevant only if actively working with masked diffusion models (e.g., Genie, Muse-variants), which are rare in production RAG/agentic systems. The attention-discounting technique could inform custom reranking logic, but the 3.1% overhead and training-free constraint limit practical applicability compared to established inference optimization strategies.
rows.entry_summary: Introduces ADAS, a training-free attention-discounted reranking method for parallel masked diffusion language model decoding. Uses soft attention penalties to discount candidates attending to uncertain already-selected positions, improving subset construction while preserving existing samplers' stopping rules. Achieves 9-10% improvement on reasoning/code benchmarks with 3.1% overhead.

rows.title: Optimal Post-Training Quantization Scales and Where to Find Them
rows.abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) compresses large language models by mapping weights to low-bit representations. The scaling factor that defines the quantization grid is typically chosen using simple, data-free heuristics. In this work, we present PiSO (Piecewise Scale Optimization), an algorithm that leverages calibration data to compute the optimal channel-wise weight scales exactly and efficiently under round-to-nearest quantization. PiSO partitions the scale search space into finitely many intervals on which the objective admits a closed-form minimizer. We extend PiSO to group-wise quantization via principled heuristics and propose effective strategies for interleaving scale optimization with error correction. Experiments on Llama and Qwen models across multiple model sizes and target weight bit-widths demonstrate consistent improvements in perplexity and downstream zero-shot accuracy, both standalone and combined with error correction. In particular, we observe increased benefits as the target bit-width narrows and quantization becomes more challenging.
rows.pre_filter_rationale: Directly applicable to production LLM deployment; PTQ is a standard compression technique for inference, and data-driven scale optimization addresses a practical bottleneck in quantization pipelines with demonstrated improvements on widely-used models.
rows.entry_relevance_reason: Post-training quantization is directly relevant to LLM inference optimization for production systems, though the contribution is algorithmic rather than addressing architectural or systems-level production concerns.
rows.entry_value_rationale: PiSO provides a practical quantization tuning method that could reduce model serving costs and latency in deployed RAG/agent systems; the integration with GPTQ and empirical validation on standard models makes it actionable for inference optimization decisions within a 6-month horizon.
rows.entry_summary: PiSO algorithm computes optimal quantization scales for post-training quantization of LLMs by partitioning scale search space into intervals with closed-form minimizers. Extends to group-wise quantization and integrates with error correction methods like GPTQ, showing consistent perplexity improvements on Llama/Qwen models.

rows.title: AuRA: Internalizing Audio Understanding into LLMs as LoRA
rows.abstract: Recent efforts to extend large language models (LLMs) to speech inputs typically rely on cascaded ASR-LLM pipelines, end-to-end speech-language models, or bridge/distillation-based adaptation. While these routes respectively reuse strong pretrained components, enable native speech-language interaction, or offer lightweight adaptation, they often suffer from transcript-interface latency, costly multimodal training, or sequential speech-language coupling. To address these limitations, we present AuRA, a method that distills audio encoding capability into the LLM. Specifically, AuRA feeds the same speech input to an ASR encoder (as a teacher) and a LoRA-adapted LLM (as a student) through a lightweight audio embedding layer, and uses layer-wise distillation to align the student's hidden states with corresponding teacher representations, thereby internalizing speech representations into lightweight LLM-side adaptations. Compared with cascaded and serial bridge methods, AuRA enables tighter speech-language joint modeling and efficient parallel end-to-end inference, while also reusing pretrained speech and language models rather than requiring large-scale multimodal training. On multiple speech-language benchmarks, AuRA consistently outperforms cascaded systems, speech-to-LLM adaptation baselines, and large-scale speech-language and multimodal models in both effectiveness and efficiency.
rows.pre_filter_rationale: Directly applicable to production speech-to-LLM pipelines; LoRA-based adaptation is lightweight and deployable, addresses real latency/cost tradeoffs in cascaded vs. end-to-end architectures, and layer-wise distillation is an actionable engineering pattern for multimodal LLM systems.
