rows.entry_relevance_reason: While this demonstrates efficient parameter adaptation via LoRA and end-to-end multimodal processing, audio understanding is tangential to core applied NLP/RAG work and the approach lacks production deployment considerations like latency, inference cost, or failure mode handling.
rows.entry_value_rationale: Potentially valuable for document intelligence pipelines that ingest audio input (e.g., meeting transcription at inference time), but the audio-specific architecture doesn't transfer to text-centric RAG, agentic systems, or document extraction workflows that define current priorities.
rows.entry_summary: AuRA internalizes audio understanding into LLMs via LoRA by distilling speech representations from an ASR teacher into lightweight low-rank adapters in early LLM layers, eliminating the need for inference-time speech encoders while enabling efficient parallel end-to-end speech-language processing.

rows.title: TRACE: A Unified Rollout Budget Allocation Framework for Efficient Agentic Reinforcement Learning
rows.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is a promising approach for enhancing reasoning and agentic behavior in large language models. However, rollout-intensive policy optimization is often limited by insufficient reward contrast, arising when overly simple or complex prompts generate low-variance feedback and when outcome-only rewards assign the same terminal assessment to every decision in a multi-turn rollout. Past efforts have focused on allocating available rollout resources to promising prompts, yet they only leverage sample informativeness at the prompt level and neglect variation in prefix-level informativeness across turns within the same rollout. This work targets multi-turn agentic RL by modeling each ReAct-style thought-action-observation turn as a semantically distinct node, allowing budget allocation to extend from prompt roots to turn-level prefixes with further continuations, which naturally forms tree-structured rollouts. We introduce Tree Rollout Allocation for Contrastive Exploration (TRACE), a unified rollout allocation framework that enhances reward contrast within a fixed sampling budget. Technically, TRACE allocates rollout budget to both prompt roots and intermediate prefixes that are most likely to yield mixed terminal rewards. A shared generalizable predictor estimates conditional success probability at these anchors from prefix histories to guide this allocation. The resulting adaptive tree structure enriches outcome-only feedback and amplifies the policy-update signal. Empirically, TRACE achieves competitive performance and efficiency gains on typical agentic benchmarks, e.g., improving Qwen3-14B Multi-Hop QA average accuracy by 2.8 points over competitive baselines at equal sampling cost.
rows.pre_filter_rationale: Directly addresses production agentic RL optimization—rollout budget allocation, reward signal quality, and multi-turn reasoning efficiency are core pain points in shipping LLM agents; TRACE's tree-structured allocation and prefix-level informativeness modeling offer actionable patterns for improving sample efficiency in multi-step reasoning systems.
rows.entry_relevance_reason: Directly addresses agent planning and budget allocation under resource constraints, but focuses on RL theory rather than practical deployment patterns for production agentic systems.
rows.entry_value_rationale: Relevant for understanding how to optimize rollout efficiency in planning-based agents and multi-step reasoning, which applies to agentic orchestration in production systems. However, the RL-centric framing and tree-search focus limits immediate applicability to LangGraph-style agent patterns used in practice.
rows.entry_summary: TRACE is a unified rollout budget allocation framework for agentic RL that allocates sampling budget to both prompt roots and intermediate prefixes most likely to yield mixed terminal rewards, enabling tree-structured rollouts with enhanced reward contrast within fixed computational budgets.

rows.title: A Unifying Lens on Supervised Fine-Tuning Through Target Distribution Design
rows.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) typically maximizes the likelihood of every token in a demonstrated trajectory. However, an observed token can be non-unique, noisy, or misaligned with the model prior. Strictly fitting toward this one-hot target may be suboptimal, especially when the pretrained model encodes a rich knowledge prior. In this work, we reinterpret SFT as target distribution design: instead of studying only the loss objective, we analyze the token-level target that the loss drives the model to match. We introduce the Q-target framework, which decomposes SFT supervision into two explicit choices: (1) how strongly to rely on the observed token, and (2) how to allocate the remaining probability mass over alternatives. This perspective unifies many existing SFT variants as implicit choices of the target distribution Q. Building on this view, we propose Target-SFT which constructs the training objective directly from the desired target distribution. This method consistently outperforms across the ten reasoning dataset-model settings evaluated, showing the effectiveness of this target-based approach. Overall, our formulation reveals a more fundamental design principle for SFT training and opens a broader search space for SFT objectives.
rows.pre_filter_rationale: Directly applicable to production SFT pipelines: the Q-target framework provides actionable design principles for improving token-level supervision in instruction-tuned models, with demonstrated empirical gains across reasoning tasks—immediately relevant for optimizing fine-tuning objectives in deployed systems.
rows.entry_relevance_reason: Provides a theoretical framework for SFT optimization with practical improvements on reasoning tasks, but lacks direct application to RAG, agentic systems, or production inference concerns.
rows.entry_value_rationale: The Q-target framework offers a principled approach to handling target distribution design during fine-tuning, which could improve model quality for document understanding and reasoning in RAG pipelines; however, the work is primarily algorithmic rather than addressing production deployment, cost, or system-level architectural decisions that typically constrain applied AI engineering.
rows.entry_summary: Proposes a unifying framework for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) via target distribution design. Introduces Q-target framework decomposing SFT into two choices: trust weight γt for observed tokens and alternative distribution π̃t for remaining probability mass. Target-SFT shows consistent improvements across reasoning datasets.

rows.title: Quantifying Subliminal Behavioral Transfer Ratios in Language Model Distillation
rows.abstract: Distillation of a language model intended to transfer benign behavior to a student model may also transfer undesirable characteristics, if they are present in the teacher model, a phenomenon known as subliminal learning. While qualitative evidence supports the existence of this effect, its magnitude has not been systematically characterized. This study quantifies subliminal behavioral transfer ratios by steering two teacher models (Llama-2-7B-Chat and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) at varying steering strengths and distilling student models using only benign data. Evaluation on 100 JailbreakBench prompts with GPT-4.1, serving as the evaluator, indicates that transfer is robust but exhibits distinct scaling behaviors. Llama-2 demonstrates a sharp threshold ($τ= {0.25,0.32} \ \text{beyond} \ α= -0.15$), whereas Qwen2.5 displays continuous and higher levels of transfer ($τ$ up to $0.61$).
rows.pre_filter_rationale: Directly addresses production concern of unintended behavior transfer in distillation pipelines—critical for safety-critical deployments—with empirical quantification of transfer ratios across models, providing actionable insights for practitioners building distilled systems.
rows.entry_relevance_reason: This paper focuses on adversarial model manipulation and jailbreak effectiveness rather than production-applicable LLM systems, evaluation frameworks, or retrieval/agentic architectures central to the profile.
rows.entry_value_rationale: The adversarial steering methodology is tangentially relevant to understanding LLM failure modes and robustness, but lacks actionable insights for building reliable production systems, RAG pipelines, or agent architectures within a 6-month engineering horizon.
rows.entry_summary: Quantifies subliminal behavioral transfer in language model distillation by steering teacher models (Llama-2, Qwen2.5) via refusal-direction activation manipulation and measuring student ASR on jailbreak prompts. Finds model-dependent scaling: Llama exhibits sharp threshold (τ=0.25-0.32 beyond α=-0.15), Qwen shows continuous transfer (τ up to 0.61).

rows.title: FlowBank: Query-Adaptive Agentic Workflows Optimization through Precompute-and-Reuse
rows.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems are increasingly powerful, but current agentic workflow optimization paradigms make an unsatisfying trade-off. Task-level methods spend substantial offline compute yet deploy only a single workflow, leaving complementary candidates unused, while query-level methods synthesize a new workflow per query at substantial inference cost. Our motivating analysis shows these paradigms are more complementary than competing: workflows discovered during offline search often solve different subsets of queries, and many queries handled by expensive query-level generation can already be solved by cheaper precomputed workflows. This suggests a different objective: rather than searching for one universally best workflow or regenerating one per instance, we should build a compact bank of reusable, complementary workflows and select among them adaptively at inference time. Doing so requires solving three coupled problems: generating complementary rather than redundant candidates, compressing them into a small deployable portfolio, and assigning each query to the right workflow under a performance-cost trade-off. To this end, we present FlowBank, a three-stage framework for portfolio-based agentic workflow optimization. Diversifying proposes DiverseFlow to steer search toward under-covered queries and produce a high-coverage candidate pool. Curating proposes CuraFlow to compress this pool into a compact portfolio with minimal redundancy. Matching casts deployment as edge-value prediction on a query-workflow bipartite graph and routes each incoming query to the portfolio member with the best predicted utility. Across five benchmarks, FlowBank achieves the highest average score among the evaluated methods while remaining cost-competitive, improving over the strongest automated and handcrafted baselines by 4.26% and 14.92% relative, respectively.
rows.pre_filter_rationale: Directly addresses core agentic workflow optimization with practical production concerns (cost-performance tradeoffs, inference latency, portfolio management), presents a concrete three-stage framework (diversity, curation, matching) with empirical validation across benchmarks—immediately actionable for multi-agent system design.
rows.entry_relevance_reason: Directly addresses agentic workflow optimization with production concerns (latency, cost) using portfolio-based routing, a pattern highly relevant to orchestrating multi-agent LLM systems at scale.
rows.entry_value_rationale: Provides a concrete architectural pattern for query-adaptive agent composition and inference-time routing that balances performance-cost tradeoffs. The precompute-and-reuse approach with bipartite matching is immediately applicable to reducing latency/cost in production agentic workflows without retraining.
rows.entry_summary: FlowBank optimizes LLM-based multi-agent workflows via portfolio-based selection. It generates diverse workflow candidates offline, compresses them into a compact bank, and routes queries adaptively at inference using bipartite graph matching to balance performance and cost.

rows.title: When Probing Accuracy Saturates, Fragility Resolves: A Complementary Metric for LLM Pre-Training Analysis
rows.abstract: Standard linear probing declares a property "encoded" when a classifier on hidden states achieves high accuracy. The protocol works well on a snapshot but breaks across pre-training: probe accuracy saturates within the first few thousand steps, leaving most of training invisible to the instrument. We introduce fragility, a complementary per-layer metric defined as the activation-noise level at which probe accuracy collapses. Fragility is sensitive to both the margin of separability and the redundancy of representation, both of which keep evolving long after accuracy plateaus. Applied to open-checkpoint language models, fragility recovers structure that accuracy alone cannot see. Moralized representations emerge along a lexical $\to$ compositional gradient: lexical moral detection first, compositional moral encoding later. Because probe accuracy on its own tracks how lexically separable a dataset is, we establish the compositional encoding directly, by showing it transfers across construction types that share no contrast tokens. A layer-depth robustness gradient develops monotonically across training while accuracy stays flat. And matched fine-tuning corpora that produce identical probing accuracy leave distinct fragility fingerprints, showing that data curation reshapes probe robustness without changing probe accuracy. In every comparison we test, where probing accuracy returns a flat answer, fragility returns a structured one.
rows.pre_filter_rationale: Directly applicable to LLM evaluation and interpretability at scale: introduces a complementary metric (fragility via activation-noise robustness) that survives the saturation problem plaguing standard probing protocols, enabling observation of representation evolution across full training trajectories—actionable for understanding when and how models develop compositional vs. lexical capabilities.
rows.entry_relevance_reason: Probing analysis and representation metrics are tangentially relevant to understanding LLM behavior, but fragility-via-noise-injection is a theoretical lens without direct application to production RAG, agentic systems, or document intelligence workflows.
rows.entry_value_rationale: Could inform model selection criteria if fragility correlates with downstream task performance in retrieval or extraction scenarios, but the paper targets pre-training analysis rather than inference-time production concerns like latency, cost, or observability that drive engineering decisions.
rows.entry_summary: Proposes fragility metric for LLM probing that measures activation-noise robustness of learned representations. When linear probing accuracy saturates early in pre-training, fragility continues evolving, revealing representational structure invisible to accuracy alone via per-layer critical noise thresholds.
rows.human_notes: pre-training and not really applied engineering; relevance score is also 0.35

rows.title: APEX: Automated Prompt Engineering eXpert with Dynamic Data Selection
rows.abstract: Large Language Models are highly sensitive to prompt formulation, necessitating automatic prompt optimization to unlock their full potential. While evolutionary algorithms have emerged as the dominant paradigm, they suffer from a critical bottleneck: data efficiency. Current methods treat the development dataset as a static benchmark, wasting significant compute budget on uninformative data. In this work, we introduce APEX (Automatic Prompt Engineering eXpert), a novel framework that optimizes the data usage alongside the prompt search. APEX dynamically stratifies the dataset into Easy, Hard, and Mixed tiers based on the optimization lineage. By prioritizing the Mixed tier, which identifies the data where the LLM has mixed performance, we identify two high-leverage subsets: the addressable frontier for generating informative mutations and the rank-sensitive frontier for distinguishing candidate quality. We evaluate APEX across three diverse benchmarks: IFBench, SimpleQA Verified, and FACTS Grounding. Under a fixed budget of 5,000 evaluation calls, due to its data efficiency, APEX outperforms the initial prompt by an average of 11.2% on Gemini 2.5 Flash and 6.8% on Gemma 3 27B, demonstrating that a data-centric approach is key to efficient and effective prompt optimization.
rows.pre_filter_rationale: Directly applicable to production prompt optimization workflows; data-efficient prompt search is a practical bottleneck in deployed RAG/agentic systems, and the dynamic stratification approach offers actionable patterns for reducing evaluation costs.
rows.entry_relevance_reason: Prompt optimization through intelligent data selection is tangentially relevant to production LLM systems, but the approach focuses on prompt mutation rather than architectural patterns or system design that would directly impact RAG/agentic workflows.
rows.entry_value_rationale: The stratified data selection strategy (prioritizing ambiguous examples where models struggle) could improve few-shot prompting in retrieval-augmented generation chains and agent tool-use contexts. However, the improvement is modest (11.2%) and the technique requires offline analysis, limiting applicability to rapidly evolving production systems where prompt patterns stabilize quickly.
rows.entry_summary: APEX optimizes prompt engineering by dynamically selecting high-leverage training data rather than treating datasets as static. It stratifies data into Easy/Hard/Mixed tiers, prioritizing Mixed examples where LLM performance is inconsistent to guide mutation and selection phases with 11.2% improvement under fixed budget.

rows.title: ISE: An Execution-Grounded Recipe for Multi-Turn OS-Agent Trajectories
rows.abstract: Training capable OS agents requires data that simultaneously captures structured user intents, multi-turn task delegation, and grounded tool execution--properties absent from existing datasets. We propose ISE (Intent -> Simulate -> Execute), a three-stage synthesis paradigm that addresses these gaps jointly. Stage 1 constructs roughly 50000 structured intents via a 4D framework (Persona x Domain x Task x Complexity); after deduplication the pool contains 43956 unique intents and attains a Vendi Score of 61.57 over the entire pool on mpnet-base-v2 embeddings (cosine kernel, q=1). Stage 2 drives multi-turn user-agent interaction through a role-locked user simulator that grounds each user turn in actual execution outcomes, producing 23132 complete trajectories averaging 8.12 user turns and 68.24 total dialogue turns. Stage 3 runs every tool call inside a live, isolated OS workspace, generating authentic failure-recovery dynamics instead of simulated responses. Fine-tuning on ISETrace improves ClawEval pass@1 from 19.3 to 37.7 using Qwen3-8B on agent tool-use tasks with a standard protocol. This result outperforms zero-shot GPT-4o and the larger Qwen3-32B base model which is four times bigger. An ablation on Stage 2 proves multi-turn simulation brings a large portion of the performance gain. We release all source code and dataset at https://github.com/Valiere01/ISE-Trace.
rows.pre_filter_rationale: Directly addresses agentic systems, multi-turn trajectory data synthesis, and tool-use evaluation—core to production agent development. The execution-grounded approach (Stage 3) and ablation methodology are practically relevant for building reliable OS agents.
rows.entry_relevance_reason: OS-agent trajectory generation is tangential to core NLP/RAG/document-focused work; while agentic systems are relevant, this focuses on GUI automation rather than LLM-driven reasoning, retrieval, or knowledge work.
rows.entry_value_rationale: The execution-grounded synthesis methodology and structured sampling approach (Persona×Domain×Task×Complexity) could inform multi-turn agent evaluation frameworks, but the OS-automation domain and ClawEval benchmark are misaligned with document intelligence, RAG systems, and knowledge-work agents that are your primary focus areas.
rows.entry_summary: ISE is a three-stage execution-grounded synthesis paradigm for generating multi-turn OS-agent trajectories: intent construction via 4D structured sampling (Persona×Domain×Task×Complexity), multi-turn role-locked user simulation with state grounding, and live OS execution validation. Produces 23,132 trajectories with authentic failure-recovery dynamics, lifting agent performance from 19.3% to 37.7% on ClawEval.

rows.title: Organize then Retrieve: Hierarchical Memory Navigation for Efficient Agents
rows.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents struggle with long-horizon tasks due to their inherent statelessness, requiring all task-relevant information to be encoded in growing input contexts. The resulting degraded reasoning quality, increased inference cost, and higher latency necessitate efficient working memory mechanisms. However, existing approaches either rely on lossy compression or similarity-based retrieval, which often fail to capture temporal structure and causal dependencies required for multi-step agentic tasks. In this work, we present HORMA, a Hierarchical Organize-and-Retrieve Memory Agent that organizes experience into a file-system-like hierarchical structure, where summarized entities are linked to the corresponding raw trajectories, enabling efficient access without losing detailed information. HORMA decomposes working memory into two stages: structured memory construction and navigation-based retrieval. The construction module iteratively refines how experiences are structured by distinguishing between failures caused by missing information and those caused by misleading or overloaded context. The navigation module retrieves task-relevant context by traversing the hierarchy using a lightweight agent trained with reinforcement learning to select minimal yet sufficient context, thereby reducing latency along the critical execution path. Across ALFWorld, LoCoMo, and LongMemEval, HORMA improves task performance under constrained context budgets while requiring at most 22.17% of the baseline token usage in long conversation tasks. Compared to existing methods, it consistently achieves better efficiency-performance trade-offs and generalizes effectively to unseen tasks.
rows.pre_filter_rationale: Directly addresses core production challenge in agentic systems—efficient memory management for long-horizon tasks—with concrete architectural pattern (hierarchical organize-retrieve) and empirical token efficiency gains demonstrating practical applicability to deployed agent systems.
rows.entry_relevance_reason: Directly addresses memory management and retrieval efficiency in agentic systems with quantified production gains (78-97% token reduction), aligning with core interests in agent orchestration and cost optimization.
rows.entry_value_rationale: Provides actionable architectural pattern for managing agent memory hierarchies and learned retrieval policies that directly reduce inference costs—critical for production long-horizon agent deployments. The decoupled memory-retrieval design offers a reusable approach for structuring agent working memory without framework lock-in.
rows.entry_summary: HORMA decouples memory construction and retrieval in LLM agents via hierarchical file-system workspace. Memory manager organizes trajectories into structured entities linked to raw data; retrieval agent navigates hierarchy using RL-trained lightweight policy to select minimal context, reducing token usage by 78-97% while maintaining performance on long-horizon tasks.

rows.title: Substrate Asymmetry in User-Side Memory: A Diagnostic Framework
rows.abstract: User-side memory in LLMs is typically scored as a single "personalization" capability: given a user's history, is the output more user-aware? We show this aggregate metric hides opposite-direction failures. Memory factorises into at least three orthogonal axes -- behavioral consistency (style, voice), factual presence (recall facts in history), and factual absence (abstain when a fact is absent) -- and no single substrate wins all three. Comparing per-user gamma-LoRA (a small LoRA adapter trained on each user's history; gamma denotes per-user, not per-task) against BGE-large dense top-K retrieval on a controlled 50-user synthetic corpus and a real-data probe (LaMP-3), we find gamma-LoRA decisively wins behavioral style while RAG decisively wins factual absence -- and the same query-projection cells in attention layers 21-35 causally load-bear both effects in opposite directions (zeroing those LoRA weights raises absence-probe TPR by +33 pp and drops presence-probe TPR by 20 pp). On the more heavily RLHF-tuned Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct the asymmetry strengthens, not heals: parametric memory's behavioral advantage collapses while its absence-calibration deficit against retrieval widens -- an alignment tax on parametric user-memory. On real-data LaMP-3, gamma-LoRA underperforms a majority baseline; a 9-condition mitigation sweep diagnoses this as instruction-following collapse, not substrate failure (a 9x2 cross-product shows the eval-time {1..5} logit mask drives main_acc to >=0.995 on every recipe), and the best training-time fix replicates bit-identically on Llama. Finally, substrate-selection routing is question-classification, not calibration: a 110M DistilBERT on the question text alone beats every logit-based router. We contribute the diagnostic framework, the diagnosed real-data negative, the alignment-tax replication, and the routing-as-classification finding.
rows.pre_filter_rationale: Directly addresses production RAG vs. parametric memory tradeoffs with diagnostic methodology, causal analysis of failure modes, and actionable routing patterns applicable to personalized LLM systems—core to practical agentic and document-aware architectures.
rows.entry_relevance_reason: Directly addresses memory architecture tradeoffs between parametric (LoRA) and retrieval-augmented approaches with empirical causal analysis, highly relevant for RAG system design decisions.
rows.entry_value_rationale: Provides actionable empirical evidence for when to apply LoRA vs. RAG in production systems and identifies specific mechanistic targets (attention layers 21–35) for optimization. The orthogonal decomposition framework helps diagnose failure modes in hybrid memory systems, directly applicable to improving Hermes-type architectures.
rows.entry_summary: Diagnostic framework decomposing user-side LLM memory into three orthogonal axes—behavioral style, factual presence, factual absence—revealing substrate asymmetry: parametric LoRA wins style (+47pp) while RAG wins absence-calibration (+90pp) on identical users. Causal mechanism localized to attention query-projection layers 21–35.

rows.title: ICA Lens: Interpreting Language Models Without Training Another Dictionary
rows.abstract: Finding interpretable directions in language-model representations is critical for understanding and controlling model behavior. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become the standard tool for this purpose, but using them as the default first lens often requires training, storing, and evaluating large overcomplete dictionaries. This bottleneck limits rapid exploration and raises a fundamental question: how much interpretable structure is already visible from activation geometry before training another neural dictionary? Our intuition is simple: many interpretable directions are selective on tokens, and these directions should look less Gaussian than random directions. We therefore revisit independent component analysis (ICA), a classical method for finding non-Gaussian directions, as a compact lens for language-model interpretability. We find that ICA has been underestimated for LLM interpretability, because prior uses often relied on off-the-shelf ICA implementations that are brittle on LLM activations and lacked systematic tools for inspecting and evaluating the recovered directions. To bridge these gaps, we introduce ICALens, the first practical workflow for stable, efficient, and auditable ICA analysis of LLM representations. It combines an optimized GPU-parallel FastICA pipeline with LLM-specific stability recipes and better fitting diagnostics, enabling efficient and reliable layer-wise analysis. Across GPT-2 Small, Gemma 2 2B, and Qwen 3.5 2B Base, ICALens efficiently recovers compact, human-interpretable directions without per-layer gradient-based dictionary training. On SAEBench, ICA is competitive with public SAEs in sparse probing and outperforms them in targeted probe perturbation under small-to-medium budgets. These results suggest that ICA should not be viewed as a weak baseline, but as an efficient and complementary first lens for exploring language-model representations.
rows.pre_filter_rationale: Directly applicable to production interpretability workflows—offers a faster, training-free alternative to SAEs for feature discovery and model debugging, reducing iteration cycles in development and enabling rapid exploration of model behavior before committing to expensive SAE training.
rows.entry_relevance_reason: While interpretability tooling has indirect value for debugging production systems, this is primarily a research methodology paper focused on representation analysis rather than solving concrete production problems in RAG, agentic systems, or document intelligence.
rows.entry_value_rationale: ICA-based interpretation could support LLM-as-judge debugging or identifying failure modes in evaluation pipelines, but the core contribution is scientific understanding of internal representations rather than architectural patterns or engineering decisions for shipping production systems.
rows.entry_summary: ICALens presents a practical workflow for using Independent Component Analysis to interpret LLM representations by finding non-Gaussian directions without training expensive sparse autoencoders. Combines optimized GPU-parallel FastICA with stability recipes and systematic evaluation across GPT-2, Gemma, and Qwen models.
rows.human_notes: How to efficiently analyze LLM internal representations; not really my niche — interesting for a quick article but other SOTA exists

rows.title: Unstable Features, Reproducible Subspaces: Understanding Seed Dependence in Sparse Autoencoders
rows.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are widely used to interpret neural network representations, but their utility depends on whether the learned features are reproducible across training runs. We study this question through \emph{feature stability}: for each SAE feature, we estimate the probability that a similar feature reappears in an independently trained SAE. This yields a scalable per-feature signal that separates stable from unstable features. In a large-scale study across seeds, models, layers, dictionary sizes, and SAE variants, we find a pronounced functional asymmetry: stable features carry most of the reconstruction- and prediction-relevant signal, while unstable features have weak marginal impact and are dominated by low-frequency surface-form triggers in both activation statistics and automatic explanations. Geometrically, unstable features are individually non-reproducible but concentrate in reproducible lower-rank subspaces, suggesting that seed dependence often reflects basis ambiguity within a shared region of activation space rather than pure noise. A controlled synthetic model makes this mechanism explicit, showing that low-rank ground-truth features can be recovered at the subspace level while remaining non-identifiable as individual SAE latents across seeds. Finally, by pooling unique cross-seed features, we construct more stable SAEs while preserving explained variance in this setting. Together, these results show that unstable features are not merely failed or noisy latents: they have weak individual functional impact, but reflect reproducible low-dimensional structure that standard SAEs resolve differently across seeds.
rows.pre_filter_rationale: Directly relevant to production interpretability systems—understanding SAE feature stability is critical for building reliable mechanistic interpretability pipelines and determining which learned features are actionable for downstream applications like anomaly detection or model debugging.
rows.entry_relevance_reason: Sparse autoencoders are interpretability research tools with limited direct application to production RAG, agentic systems, or document intelligence pipelines that form your core work.
rows.entry_value_rationale: While mechanistic interpretability of neural networks has tangential relevance to understanding LLM behavior in production systems, this work focuses on SAE internals rather than actionable patterns for system design, deployment, or debugging—the practitioner concerns that anchor your profile.
rows.entry_summary: Large-scale study of sparse autoencoder (SAE) feature reproducibility across training seeds. Shows stable features carry reconstruction/prediction signal while unstable features reflect basis ambiguity in reproducible low-rank subspaces rather than pure noise. Proposes per-feature stability metrics and constructs more stable SAEs via cross-seed feature pooling.

rows.title: ALIGNBEAM : Inference-Time Alignment Transfer via Cross-Vocabulary Logit Mixing
rows.abstract: Domain fine-tuning degrades the safety of large language models: fine-tuned specialists readily comply with harmful prompts framed in domain language. Existing inference-time defenses that mix logits from a safe anchor model require both models to share a vocabulary, which rules them out for the cross-family specialists where safety is most degraded. We present ALIGNBEAM, a training-free method that lifts this restriction by translating anchor logits into the target model's vocabulary token-by-token at each decoding step; a small LLM judge then selects the safest among K candidate continuations. No weights are changed, and the safety-utility trade-off can be tuned at deployment without retraining. Across both cross-vocabulary and same-vocabulary evaluation pairs, ALIGNBEAM substantially raises refusal on adversarial benchmarks while keeping task accuracy and inference overhead within practical bounds. The results show that safety alignment can be transferred between model families at inference time, without touching either model's weights.
rows.pre_filter_rationale: Production-relevant inference-time safety defense with practical deployment constraints (cross-vocabulary compatibility, tunable safety-utility tradeoff, no retraining), directly applicable to production LLM systems where domain fine-tuning creates safety degradation.
rows.entry_relevance_reason: This paper addresses safety alignment transfer at inference time through a novel logit-mixing technique, but lacks direct application to core RAG, agentic systems, document intelligence, or retrieval workflows.
rows.entry_value_rationale: While the cross-vocabulary logit bridging technique is technically interesting for serving heterogeneous model ensembles, it primarily solves a safety/alignment problem rather than a production ML systems problem relevant to document processing pipelines, retrieval, or agent orchestration. The inference-time constraint and vocabulary-bridging focus have limited applicability to the practitioner's core domains.
rows.entry_summary: AlignBeam enables inference-time safety alignment transfer across models with different vocabularies via cross-vocabulary logit bridge mixing (LBM), blending anchor model distributions through text-based token translation without requiring shared tokenizers or retraining.

rows.title: Quickest Detection of Hallucination Onset: Delay Bounds and Learned CUSUM Statistics
rows.abstract: Token-level hallucination detectors are evaluated as classifiers, by AUC over all tokens, yet a streaming monitor is judged by its reaction time: the number of tokens that pass between the onset of a hallucination and the alarm. We formulate hallucination onset detection as a quickest change detection problem. A first-order Markov model of the latent faithful/hallucinated state, validated on RAGTruth, places the task inside classical change-point theory and yields Lorden's lower bound on detection delay: about 1.3 tokens at a false-alarm rate of 0.01. We then show that a causal recurrent labeler acts as a CUSUM with a learned increment; at a matched false-alarm rate it detects in 11-13 tokens, against 31 for a linear per-token baseline, and a controlled decomposition attributes most of this advantage to a better per-token score rather than to temporal accumulation. An information-rate optimality theorem of Donsker-Varadhan type explains the remaining order-of-magnitude gap: the learned score realizes only 1/4.5 of the divergence the features carry, a deficit that recalibration cannot remove, with the remainder a finite-horizon effect. Classification metrics conceal this delay structure; sequential analysis makes it measurable
rows.pre_filter_rationale: Directly addresses production concern in LLM systems (hallucination detection latency), applies classical change-point theory to a practically relevant problem, and provides actionable insights on detection delay bounds and monitoring strategies relevant to production RAG/agentic systems.
rows.entry_relevance_reason: Addresses hallucination detection with theoretical rigor and establishes practical bounds, but focuses on statistical change-point theory rather than production mitigation strategies or architectural solutions.
rows.entry_value_rationale: The 1.3-token detection delay and CUSUM formulation provide a theoretical foundation for understanding when hallucinations *begin*, useful for observability systems. However, most production value lies in prevention (retrieval grounding, decoding constraints) or runtime mitigation (intermediate verification), not detection latency—making this primarily a monitoring/eval concern rather than core system design.
rows.entry_summary: Formulates hallucination detection as quickest change-point detection, establishes Lorden delay bounds (~1.3 tokens at 1% false-alarm rate), shows causal RNNs act as learned CUSUM statistics, and attributes remaining gaps to information-rate deficits rather than architecture.

rows.title: Keep Policy Gradient in Charge: Sibling-Guided Credit Distillation for Long-Horizon Tool-Use Agents
rows.abstract: Long-horizon tool-use reinforcement learning can learn from outcome verification, but its trajectory-level advantage is broadcast across many reasoning, API, and answer tokens. Self-distillation promises a denser signal by reusing a policy's own rollouts or a privileged teacher. We show, however, that direct token-level self-distillation can silently destroy tool use: it rehearses teacher behavior without knowing which actions the verifier rewards, so useful skills and harmful shortcuts are amplified together. We introduce Sibling-Guided Credit Distillation (SGCD), which uses distillation for credit assignment rather than as a competing actor loss. Dynamic sampling produces mixed successful and failed sibling rollouts; an external LLM summarizes their contrast into a training-only stepwise credit reference; dense teacher/student divergence drives credit reassignment; and bounded detached credit weights reshape GRPO token advantages. The deployed student sees no external LLM, sibling evidence, or oracle. Across AppWorld and $τ^3$-airline, SGCD improves over matched GRPO comparators: AppWorld TGC $42.9 \to 45.6$ on test_normal and $24.7 \to 27.0$ on test_challenge, and $τ^3$-airline pass@1 $0.583 \to 0.602$.
rows.pre_filter_rationale: Directly addresses credit assignment in long-horizon agentic RL with tool use—a production pain point—proposing a practical distillation technique (SGCD) that avoids pitfalls of naive self-distillation and demonstrates gains on standard benchmarks; relevant to building reliable multi-step agent systems.
rows.entry_relevance_reason: While addressing agent tool-use and credit assignment in RL, the paper focuses on reinforcement learning optimization rather than production agentic system architecture, retrieval integration, or deployment concerns central to applied work.
rows.entry_value_rationale: Potentially useful if building RL-based agents with long-horizon planning, but most production agentic systems (LangGraph, multi-turn orchestration) rely on LLM reasoning and tool-use patterns rather than policy gradient methods; the techniques are research-stage RL optimization without demonstrated production deployment patterns.
rows.entry_summary: SGCD addresses zero-tool collapse in long-horizon agent RL by using sibling-guided credit distillation instead of competing distillation losses. Divergence-driven credit weighting reshapes GRPO advantages while keeping policy gradient dominant, avoiding teacher-student misalignment that destroys tool-use behavior.

rows.title: Zero-source LLM Hallucination Detection with Human-like Criteria Probing
rows.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often hallucinate by generating factually incorrect or unfaithful content, posing significant risks to their safe use. Detecting such hallucinations is particularly challenging under the zero-source constraint, where no model internals or external references are available, and detection must rely solely on the textual query-answer pair. In this paper, we propose Human-like Criteria Probing for Hallucination Detection (HCPD), a paradigm that emulates the multi-faceted reasoning of human evaluators. Its core is a Human-like Criteria Probing (HCP) mechanism, in which a LLM agent adaptively decomposes its judgment into a weighted set of interpretable criteria and aggregates criterion-specific scores into a final truthfulness measure. To achieve this adaptive capability, we introduce a reward-based alignment scheme using only weak supervision from semantic consistency. At inference, we employ a multi-sampling aggregation strategy to ensure robust decisions while preserving full interpretability. We further provide theoretical analysis supporting the reliability of our approach. Extensive experiments show that HCPD consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, offering an effective and explainable solution for zero-source hallucination detection. Code is available at https://github.com/TRISKEL10N/HCPD.
rows.pre_filter_rationale: Zero-source hallucination detection is a critical production concern for RAG and agentic systems where external verification is unavailable; the adaptive criteria decomposition and multi-sampling aggregation approach directly addresses observability and interpretability requirements in deployed LLM applications.
rows.entry_relevance_reason: Directly addresses hallucination detection—a critical production concern in RAG and agentic systems—with a practical zero-source approach that scales without external references.
rows.entry_value_rationale: The interpretable criteria decomposition and weak-supervision training method is actionable for building reliable LLM-as-judge evaluators in production pipelines. The zero-source design fits well into RAG systems where factuality checking against retrieved context is essential, reducing dependency on specialized models or APIs.
rows.entry_summary: Proposes HCPD, a zero-source hallucination detection framework that emulates human evaluators by adaptively decomposing judgments into weighted interpretable criteria, using reward-based alignment training with weak supervision and multi-sampling aggregation for robust, explainable detection without model internals or external references.

rows.title: MiniPIC: Flexible Position-Independent Caching in <100LOC
rows.abstract: Retrieval-augmented and agentic workloads repeatedly prefill recurring predictable structured inputs (which we call "spans") such as documents and code files. Yet, prefix caching in engines such as vLLM cannot reuse their KV entries unless they share identical prefixes with another request, while Position-Independent Caching (PIC) implementations within production-grade inference servers typically either require substantial server code changes or keep KV state outside the server, incurring host-to-device transfer overhead. We present Minimalistic PIC (MiniPIC): a minimal, flexible and fast vLLM design built from two ingredients: positional-encoding-free KV cache and user-controlled cache-reuse primitives. MiniPIC stores unrotated K vectors in the KV cache, applies RoPE to K tiles inside attention using per-request logical positions, and exposes three user-facing and token-level primitives: block-aligned padding, span separator (SSep), and prompt depend (PDep), that modify hashing behavior and effective block-level causal attention structure. With fewer than 100 lines of core-engine changes plus a custom attention backend, these primitives are sufficient to realize multiple PIC methods, including Block-Attention, EPIC, and Prompt Cache, within the same running vLLM instance, while natively integrating with KV cache CPU offload implementations. On 2WikiMultihopQA, MiniPIC with interleaved scheduling improves prefill throughput by 49% over baseline vLLM, reduces cached-span time-to-first-token by up to two orders of magnitude, preserves the linear prefill scaling of uncached spans, and incurs only 5.7% worst-case overhead.
rows.pre_filter_rationale: Directly addresses production RAG/agentic inference optimization (prefix caching reuse across structured inputs) with minimal implementation overhead, clear engineering tradeoffs, and measured production impact on throughput and latency.
rows.entry_relevance_reason: Directly addresses production KV cache optimization in vLLM with practical engineering focused on latency and resource efficiency, though primarily a serving infrastructure concern rather than core NLP/RAG system design.
rows.entry_value_rationale: Reduces inference latency and memory footprint through intelligent cache reuse patterns—critical for production deployment at scale. The position-independent caching approach enables better resource utilization across concurrent requests, directly improving cost/throughput tradeoffs in served LLM systems. Minimal implementation complexity (<100 LOC) makes it deployable within existing production stacks.
rows.entry_summary: MiniPIC enables flexible position-independent KV cache reuse in vLLM through position-free cache storage and user-controlled primitives (padding, SSep, PDep), requiring <100 LOC changes. Applies RoPE in-kernel to support concurrent span reuse across requests without positional conflicts.

rows.title: MemRefine: LLM-Guided Compression for Long-Term Agent Memory
rows.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly expected to operate over long-term interactions, where information from past dialogues must be preserved and recalled to support future tasks. However, as interactions accumulate, the memory store grows without bound and fills with redundant entries that inflate storage cost and degrade retrieval by crowding out the most useful evidence. Furthermore, this is especially limiting on resource-constrained platforms with hard memory budgets, motivating us to formulate storage-budgeted memory management, the task of keeping an already constructed memory store within a fixed budget while preserving information useful for future interactions. To this end, we then propose MemRefine, an LLM-guided framework that, since surface similarity poorly reflects factual value, uses similarity only to propose candidate pairs and defers delete, merge, and preserve decisions to an LLM judge based on factual content, iterating until the budget is met. Across multiple memory frameworks and long-term conversation benchmarks, MemRefine consistently meets target budgets while preserving downstream performance and outperforming rule-based baselines under tight budgets.
rows.pre_filter_rationale: Directly addresses production-critical problem of long-term agent memory management with practical LLM-guided compression strategy; highly relevant to agentic systems and memory architectures in resource-constrained deployments.
rows.entry_relevance_reason: Directly addresses a core agentic systems challenge—scalable memory management for long-horizon agents—with a practical LLM-guided approach that improves on heuristic baselines.
rows.entry_value_rationale: Provides an actionable pattern for production agents that need persistent memory beyond context windows, addressing a known pain point in multi-turn reasoning systems. The hybrid similarity + LLM reasoning approach is immediately applicable to long-running agent architectures.
rows.entry_summary: MemRefine proposes LLM-guided compression for long-term agent memory within fixed storage budgets. Uses similarity-based candidate selection paired with LLM factual reasoning to make delete/merge/preserve decisions, outperforming rule-based approaches on conversation benchmarks.

rows.title: Reward Modeling for Multi-Agent Orchestration
rows.abstract: Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) built on Large Language Models (LLMs) require effective orchestration to coordinate specialized agents, yet training such orchestrators is hindered by limited supervision and high computational cost. We propose Orchestration Reward Modeling (OrchRM), a self-supervised framework for evaluating orchestration quality without human annotations. OrchRM leverages intermediate artifacts from multi-agent executions to construct win-lose pairs for Bradley-Terry reward model training. Unlike existing MAS test-time scaling and orchestrator training frameworks that rely on costly sub-agent rollouts, OrchRM operates directly at the orchestration level, enabling efficient and high-performing reward-guided orchestrator training and MAS test-time scaling. OrchRM improves training efficiency by up to 10x in token usage while improving MAS test-time scaling performance by up to 8% in accuracy. These gains consistently transfer across multiple domains, including mathematical reasoning, web-based question answering, and multi-hop reasoning, demonstrating orchestration-level reward modeling as a scalable direction for robust multi-agent orchestration. Code will be available at https://github.com/Wang-ML-Lab/OrchRM.
rows.pre_filter_rationale: Directly applicable to agentic orchestration workflows; addresses production concern of efficient multi-agent coordination without costly human annotation; demonstrates concrete efficiency gains (10x token reduction) and performance improvements across domains relevant to practical RAG/agent systems.
rows.entry_relevance_reason: Directly addresses agentic orchestration and training efficiency, with practical production implications for multi-agent systems, though reward modeling novelty is secondary to architectural applicability.
rows.entry_value_rationale: Provides a concrete self-supervised approach to training agent orchestrators without human annotation overhead—a production bottleneck—and demonstrates measurable efficiency gains relevant to scaling reasoning workloads. The intermediate artifact usage pattern is architecturally transferable to existing LangGraph-based systems.
rows.entry_summary: OrchRM: Self-supervised reward modeling framework for multi-agent LLM orchestration using intermediate artifacts to train Bradley-Terry models. Enables efficient orchestrator training without human annotations, achieving 10x token efficiency gains and 8% accuracy improvements in test-time scaling across reasoning domains.

rows.title: Beyond the Commitment Boundary: Probing Epiphenomenal Chain-of-Thought in Large Reasoning Models
rows.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning is the dominant paradigm for inference-time scaling in language models, yet the causal influence of individual steps on the final answer poorly understood. We estimate each step's causal importance via early exit and use this measure to study how answers form across the reasoning traces of several model families. Across diverse tasks, we find that reasoning typically crosses a \emph{commitment boundary} -- a sharp transition from transient intermediate guesses to a stable, high-confidence answer. This transition often happens in a single step, well before the model's reasoning block ends, and is followed by \emph{epiphenomenal} CoT steps that leave the final answer probability unaltered. Using attention probes, we show that answer-formation stages can be linearly decoded from intermediate reasoning steps with high accuracy and generalize robustly to unseen reasoning tasks. We exploit this signal to early-exit reasoning blocks at the commitment boundary, reducing the length of CoTs up to 55\% on average with negligible impact on model performance.
rows.pre_filter_rationale: Directly applicable to production inference cost optimization: early-exit mechanics for CoT reduce latency/tokens by 55% without performance loss, with clear implementation path via attention probes and commitment boundary detection.
rows.entry_relevance_reason: While the paper offers insights into CoT efficiency that could optimize inference latency in production systems, it is primarily a theoretical analysis of model internals rather than an architectural pattern or engineering framework applicable to building RAG/agentic systems.
rows.entry_value_rationale: The 55% CoT length reduction finding could inform latency optimization decisions in cost-sensitive deployments, but the work lacks guidance on integrating these insights into production pipelines, agent orchestration, or retrieval-augmented workflows—the core domains of current work.
rows.entry_summary: Analyzes causal influence of chain-of-thought steps in reasoning models via early exit and attention probes, revealing commitment boundaries where answers stabilize before epiphenomenal steps occur, enabling 55% CoT length reduction without performance loss.

rows.title: SkMTEB: Slovak Massive Text Embedding Benchmark and Model Adaptation
rows.abstract: We introduce SkMTEB, the first comprehensive MTEB-style text embedding benchmark for Slovak, a low-resource West Slavic language, comprising 31 datasets across 7 task types -- nearly 4$\times$ the depth of existing multilingual benchmark coverage for Slovak. Our evaluation of 31 embedding models reveals that large instruction-tuned multilingual models achieve the strongest performance, while existing Slovak-specific models trained for NLU tasks transfer poorly to embedding tasks. To address the need for efficient, locally-deployable Slovak embeddings, we develop \texttt{e5-sk-small} (45M parameters) and \texttt{e5-sk-large} (365M) by applying vocabulary trimming and fine-tuning to Multilingual E5 models. Despite size reductions of up to 62\%, our open-source models achieve competitive performance with proprietary APIs while remaining locally deployable for semantic search and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). We release the benchmark, models, datasets, and code openly, hoping our approach offers a replicable path for other under-resourced languages.
rows.pre_filter_rationale: Directly relevant: embedding model evaluation, benchmark design, and fine-tuning methodology applicable to RAG/retrieval systems; vocabulary trimming and model adaptation techniques useful for production deployment constraints.
rows.entry_relevance_reason: While embedding model optimization is relevant to RAG systems, this work is narrowly focused on Slovak-language benchmarking without addressing general architectural patterns, retrieval strategies, or production deployment considerations applicable across languages.
rows.entry_value_rationale: Useful reference for understanding embedding model compression techniques (vocabulary trimming, fine-tuning for size reduction) that could inform similar optimizations for other low-resource languages in RAG pipelines, but limited applicability to English-dominant production systems and no insights into hybrid retrieval, reranking, or integration patterns.
rows.entry_summary: SkMTEB introduces the first comprehensive Slovak text embedding benchmark with 31 datasets across 7 task types, plus vocabulary-trimmed and fine-tuned E5 models (45M–365M parameters) achieving competitive performance with 62% size reduction for practical low-resource language deployment.
